item.title: Spatial Nonlocality from Finite Extinction Ratio in BOTDR over Heterogeneous Fiber Links
item.description: arXiv:2610.14128v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Finite extinction ratio in pulse-modulated Brillouin optical time-domain reflectometry (BOTDR) produces residual inter-pulse Brillouin backscatter outside the nominal pulse gate. We model and experimentally quantify this effect as spatial nonlocality in a heterogeneous fiber link and define the spectral contamination ratio (SCR) as the contaminating Brillouin-band power normalized to the local Brillouin-band power. Measurements were performed using a 1.2 km standard single-mode fiber (SMF) followed by 0.1 km of dispersion-compensating fiber (DCF), whose separated Brillouin frequency shifts allow section-to-section leakage to be resolved spectrally. At 20 m spatial resolution, increasing the extinction ratio from 18.5 to 33.0 dB reduced the SMF-band contamination in the DCF gates from -5.3 to -14.8 dB. Over the 16-33 dB range, the SCR showed fitted slopes of -1.064 and -1.246 dB/dB for the two contamination directions. These results quantify finite-ER-induced spatial nonlocality and provide a link-specific metric for extinction-ratio selection in BOTDR.

item.title: Definition of Multi-Parameter Super-Resolution for Optical Telescopes
item.description: arXiv:2610.14286v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Super-resolution techniques in microscopy are opening new frontiers in biology, and super-resolution for telescope imaging may provide similar benefits for astronomy and space domain awareness. Telescope super-resolution techniques such as multi-plane light conversion and photonic lanterns have been inspired by the ability of mode sorting measurements to extract classical Fisher information closer to the quantum bound than standard telescope imaging. Fisher information analyses for super-resolution imaging systems commonly consider the case of imaging point sources, but often only consider estimating a small subset of the parameters. Furthermore, there has been no demonstration of an estimation algorithm with performance that follows the limit set by the Fisher information when all point source parameters are considered. We provide a framework for defining and analyzing super-resolution using the classical and quantum Fisher information for the multi-parameter estimation problem and demonstrate an algorithm that can achieve the classical Fisher information bound for all the parameters simultaneously.

item.title: Fast local field calculation in cascaded coupled systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.14314v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Computing the field within a sub-unit of cascaded systems is a recurring problem in wave physics. It is central to gradient-based inverse design, in situations where only a region of the system is modified while the rest remains fixed. Standard approaches either resimulate the entire cascade at every change, or require a detailed characterization of every surrounding sub-system. Both become impractical when many design iterations are needed. Here, we introduce a hybrid method combining the $S$-matrix approach, which propagates fields through cascaded systems, with the Green's function method, which gives the field generated by a source within a characterized system. In this approach, the sub-systems surrounding the region of interest need only be characterized once, after which the local field can be recomputed rapidly for any new configuration. We validate the method on a disordered lossy waveguide, finding excellent agreement with finite-element simulations. We also demonstrate its efficiency on a disordered multimode cavity, where it achieves a fifty-fold speed-up over full-wave simulation and reduces a wideband focusing calculation from eleven hours to ten minutes. This approach opens the way to fast, iterative field calculations in complex systems coupled to their environment, with direct applications to inverse design and wideband wavefront-shaping.

item.title: A Portable Optical Frequency Comb with Low Repetition-Rate Drift Based on "Optical Cubes"
item.description: arXiv:2610.14490v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We demonstrate a compact, fully stabilized, all-polarization-maintaining (all-PM) Er:fiber optical frequency comb (OFC) implemented on a silica optical-cube platform. The optical comb module, including the oscillator, amplifier, spectral-broadening stage, 780-nm frequency-doubling branch, and f-to-2f interferometer, occupies a volume of 0.88 L. Without active temperature control, the free-running repetition frequency exhibits a peak-to-peak excursion of 75 Hz over 10 h, corresponding to 0.375 ppm. Under the same laboratory conditions, this excursion is 6.2 times smaller than that of a mechanically mounted non-PM reference comb. The amplified pulses are compressed to 94 fs and spectrally broadened in a PM highly nonlinear fiber. A coherent-population-trapping-based chip-scale atomic clock is employed for the first time as the radio-frequency reference for comb locking, thereby reducing the footprint of the microwave-reference subsystem. The resulting in-loop, optical-frequency-normalized tracking instability reaches 6.03E-17 at 1 s and 2.57E-18 at 10,000 s. These results demonstrate a compact comb architecture with reduced sensitivity to environmental perturbations, providing a practical route toward portable optical atomic clocks.

item.title: Maximal Axion Optical Chirality Enabled by Degenerate Quasibound States in the Continuum
item.description: arXiv:2610.14611v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Axion quasiparticles introduce magnetoelectric coupling in topological materials, yet their optical signatures are intrinsically weak, severely limiting experimental detection and practical exploitation. Here, we demonstrate maximal optical chirality of axion quasiparticles by coupling them with degenerate quasibound states in the continuum (qBICs). By integrating three-dimensional topological insulators (3DTIs) with achiral photonic crystal slabs (PCSs), we reveal that axion quasiparticles induce an effective Zeeman effect that lifts the degeneracy of achiral qBICs in PCSs, splitting them into two nondegenerate high-Q chiral qBICs with maximally opposite chirality. These result in a more than 10^3- and 200-fold increase in the polarization conversion efficiency and Faraday rotation angle, respectively, compared to the intrinsic chiroptical response of bare 3DTI films. Moreover, circular dichroism and nonreciprocal optical responses are revealed as new key signatures for probing axion quasiparticles in 3DTI-PCS coupled systems. Our results provide a definitive route for observing axion quasiparticles and topological physics, while establishing a promising platform for controlling optical polarization, spin, phase, and nonreciprocal responses.

item.title: Near-focus intensity evolution of spatiotemporal optical vortex pulses and consequences for their nonlinear upconversion
item.description: arXiv:2610.14640v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spatiotemporal optical vortex (STOV) laser pulses are attracting attention for their puzzling transverse orbital angular momentum (OAM) and propagation properties, which could determine their future applications. While the characteristic reshaping of their space-time envelope upon diffraction from the focal plane to the far-field is now well-established, the evolution of their intensity as they propagate has not been studied quantitatively, despite growing interest for their use in nonlinear optics and strong-field physics. Here, we explore experimentally and analytically the focusing dynamics of STOVs produced by a pulse shaper, and evidence a substantial longitudinal shift between the coordinate at which a circularly-symmetric STOV forms and that at which the pulse reaches its peak intensity. To illustrate some practical consequences for applications, we experimentally demonstrate how the yield of second-harmonic generation can consequently be maximized several Rayleigh lengths beyond the plane where the circular STOV really occurs. These results signal careful characterization of spatiotemporal pulses as a requisite for nonlinear optical experiments, and pave the way for finer control of complex laser drivers for light-matter interactions.

item.title: Selective spatiotemporal mode-locking in multimode Mamyshev oscillators
item.description: arXiv:2610.14690v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spatiotemporal mode-locking (STML) in multimode fibers introduces spatial degrees of freedom for ultrashort pulse generation, yet flexible manipulation of transverse mode compositions within multimode solitons remains challenging. Here, we propose a spectrum-to-mode mapping strategy in multimode Mamyshev oscillators (MOs) to selectively synchronize specific transverse modes through synergistic cross-phase modulation and offset spectral filtering. Meanwhile, four-wave mixing acts to stabilize intermodal phase relationships, facilitating selective STML characterized by diverse mode compositions with matched group velocities. Spatiotemporal solitons containing the pure LP01 mode, degenerate LP11 modes, or LP02+LP21 composite modes are selectively realized and mapped across the parameter space spanned by intracavity gain and filter detuning. Furthermore, intracavity collisions between coexisting mode groups with disparate group velocities are demonstrated to enable dynamic mode selection. Beyond the simulation of six modes in graded-index multimode fibers, selective STML is also demonstrated in MOs based on step-index multimode fibers and fibers supporting more transverse modes, confirming the generality of our approach. This strategy offers a versatile and robust pathway for transverse mode regulation and provides new insights into full dimensional structured light manipulation in multimode ultrafast fiber lasers.

item.title: Ultra-low-loss Ta2O5 waveguide for integrated nonlinear photonics
item.description: arXiv:2610.14878v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Integrated nonlinear photonics demands waveguides that simultaneously offer ultra-low-loss, relatively strong nonlinearity, and tight mode confinement. Tantalum pentoxide (Ta2O5) is attractive for this purpose because it combines a broad transparency window, relatively strong third-order nonlinearity, and favorable thick-film growth characteristics. In tightly confined Ta2O5 waveguides, however, enhanced interaction between the optical mode and etched sidewalls makes scattering loss an important limitation for achieving high Q anomalous-dispersion resonators. Here, we mitigate this confinement-scattering trade-off in pure Ta2O5 waveguides using a fabrication flow based on the Damascene concept. The resulting microring resonators (MRRs) with a cross-section of 1.6 {\mu}m x 0.85 {\mu}m exhibit intrinsic quality factors exceeding 4.0 x 106, corresponding to propagation losses below 10 dB/m, while maintaining anomalous dispersion suitable for bright dissipative Kerr soliton operation. Using these resonators, we generate a coherent bright single-soliton microcomb with a repetition rate of 108.32 GHz. Under optimized dual-pump operating conditions, the platform further exhibits an experimentally accessible single-soliton window spanning 7.5 GHz, indicating a large detuning tolerance for soliton operation; this broad operating window is consistent with the relatively weak thermo-optic response of Ta2O5. Thermal-bistability analysis further indicates that the residual scattering loss is comparable to the material-absorption loss, rather than dominating the loss budget. These results demonstrate that low optical loss, tight mode confinement, and dispersion engineering suitable for soliton formation can be jointly achieved in a pure Ta2O5 platform, providing an ultra-low-loss platform foundation for integrated nonlinear photonic devices and more complex chip-scale nonlinear photonic systems.

item.title: Resonant dispersive wave emission: a route toward few-cycle, tunable strong-field drivers in the visible
item.description: arXiv:2610.15108v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Intense ultrafast lasers are the backbone of strong-field physics and enable table-top scale applications of coherent high-photon energy radiation through high-harmonic generation (HHG). Using short-wavelength drivers in HHG promises highly efficient conversion into the extreme ultraviolet, but short pulse durations are essential to this approach. We generate multi-GW peak power, sub-10 fs pulses in the visible with broad spectral tunability (220--752 nm) by harnessing soliton dynamics in large-core, gas-filled capillary fibers for high-energy resonant dispersive wave emission. This establishes the potential of resonant dispersive waves as a new class of driving lasers for HHG and strong-field physics in addition to widespread applications in ultrafast spectroscopy.

item.title: Observation of quadrature-dependent unidirectional flow of light
item.description: arXiv:2610.15116v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Unidirectional transport of light is a central capability in photonics, enabling critical functionalities such as isolation and routing. Ordinarily, this directionality depends on the mode of light, but not its phase. In this work, we experimentally demonstrate phase-dependent unidirectional transport of light for the first time. Specifically, we realize a system where conjugate quadratures of an optical field decouple and propagate in opposite directions. Our all-optical approach uses multiple pump frequencies in a high-$Q$ nanophotonic micro-resonator to achieve Hamiltonian programming through Kerr nonlinearity. Even though we rely on optical nonlinearity, our approach is not limited to any minimal power requirement on the signal. We demonstrate the ultimate limit of this by measuring the effect of quadrature-dependent transport on vacuum fluctuations. Our approach unlocks a fundamental new capability for controlling light, and can enable previously inaccessible regimes of phase-sensitive directional amplification, sensing, and routing.

item.title: Dual deconvolution multifocal fluorescence response matrix microscopy for aberration-free high-throughput super-resolution imaging
item.description: arXiv:2610.15264v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fluorescence response matrix imaging enables separate computational correction of excitation and emission aberrations through dual deconvolution, but single-focus acquisition requires a large number of camera frames, limiting its practical use. Multifocal excitation can accelerate acquisition by recording many illumination positions in parallel, but denser foci also increase inter-focus crosstalk, which can bias the estimated excitation and emission optical transfer functions and degrade aberration correction. Here, we introduce high-throughput aberration-free fluorescence response matrix imaging with adaptive multifocal illumination, in which the inter-focus spacing of the multifocal lattice is adjusted according to specimen-dependent crosstalk. A programmable digital micromirror device generates multifocal excitation lattices, and the resulting detector-resolved fluorescence responses are assembled into a two-coordinate fluorescence response matrix. Dual deconvolution separately estimates and corrects the excitation and emission optical transfer functions, and the aberration-corrected matrix is then combined in the spatial-frequency domain to reconstruct the aberration-free image. This strategy reduces the number of required camera frames by approximately three orders of magnitude, allowing response matrices with $\sim 10^6$ illumination positions to be acquired within seconds to a few minutes. The accelerated acquisition preserves the aberration-correction capability of dual deconvolution and achieves an estimated lateral resolution of $\sim$100 nm. Applied to heterogeneous mouse brain and kidney tissue, the method enables high-resolution, depth-resolved volumetric imaging while correcting specimen-dependent aberrations. Together, these results establish adaptive multifocal illumination as a practical route to high-throughput aberration-free fluorescence response matrix imaging.

item.title: Comparative Robustness of Mach-Zehender and Microring Photonic Matrix Multipliers Under Laser RIN and Thermal Drift
item.description: arXiv:2610.15400v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Photonic matrix multipliers can accelerate neural-network inference, but their practical utility depends on how optical weight elements respond to source noise, thermal variation, and calibration error. This paper compares Mach-Zehnder modulator (MZM) and microring-resonator (MRR) implementations under laser relative-intensity noise (RIN), column-wise thermal/phase drift, and their joint action. Two CIFAR-10 classifiers - a compact four-layer CNN and ResNet-8 - are mapped to matched photonic multiply-accumulate chains using common source-distribution, detection, numerical, and calibration assumptions. Both architectures reproduce the same zero-perturbation baseline for each workload: 79.5% classification accuracy for the Small CNN and 70.0% for ResNet-8. Robustness is then evaluated using separate RIN-only and drift-only sweeps and a full two-dimensional RIN-drift grid, with dimensionless RMS perturbation levels extending from 0.5% to 20%. The analysis reports classification accuracy, class normalized confusion matrices, rolling-accuracy traces, one-dimensional robustness curves, and multidimensional response surfaces. Device equations and parameter definitions follow the models implemented in the QPI Labs Photonic Inference Simulator, with shared laser fluctuations propagated as correlated multiplicative noise and slow drift represented as a per-output-column perturbation of calibrated weights. All numerical results are generated from recorded experiment configurations and random seeds. The study provides a controlled system-level framework for comparing interferometric and resonant photonic weight elements while limiting conclusions to the implemented device models, perturbation ranges, calibration policy, and neural-network workloads.
item.dc:creator: Andreas Falkenberg

item.title: From Microresonator to Packaged Microcomb System: Fiber-Coupled Module and System Integration
item.description: arXiv:2610.15519v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We demonstrate a compact and robust soliton microcomb source designed for field-deployable operation. A directly fiber-coupled SiN microresonator was integrated with precise thermal control into a palm-sized module, reducing the footprint and volume by 16- and 81-fold, respectively. The module, together with the laser sources and optical amplifiers required for microcomb generation, was further integrated into a 19-inch rack-mounted enclosure, achieving system-level footprint and volume reductions of 2.3- and 3.7-fold, respectively. The packaged system achieved a 90% manual startup success rate and maintained continuous soliton operation for 18.8 days, while remaining operational under substantial temperature variations. A state-based automated startup scheme using discrete microcomb-state evaluation achieved single-soliton generation without manual intervention with success rates of 50% within 2 min and 60% within 3 min. Moreover, automated soliton initiation and sustained operation were demonstrated while the packaged microresonator module was directly subjected to random mechanical vibration. These results provide a practical platform for compact, robust, and field-deployable microcomb sources.
item.dc:creator: Yudai Matsumura, Yoshihiro Makimoto, Tsutomu Mizuguchi, Masayuki Higaki, Yu Tokizane, Naoya Kuse, Takeshi Yasui

item.title: Tornado Wave-Encoded Point Spread Functions for Multi-Period Three-Dimensional Localization Imaging
item.description: arXiv:2610.15606v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) localization microscopy using rotational point spread functions (PSFs) is fundamentally challenged by limited axial range, poor PSF compactness, and depth-decoding ambiguity -- particularly in dense specimens with heavy PSF overlap. To address these limitations, we introduce a 3D localization approach based on tornado wave (ToW)-PSFs, combined with a convolutional neural network (CNN) designed to decode continuous rotational patterns and resolve multi-period axial ambiguity. Our engineered PSF encodes the 3D position of each nanoparticle into a compact double-lobe pattern whose orientation rotates with axial position. This design yields a clean, well-defined structural evolution across an unprecedented 15 um axial range, with an average rotation rate of 21.8 degrees/um, ensuring robust long-range depth encoding. To recover coordinates from overlapping emitters, we systematically benchmark a conventional matching-pursuit (MP) algorithm against our CNN. While MP performs adequately in sparse scenes, the CNN demonstrates exceptional robustness in dense fields, achieving a 70.24% localization accuracy at 20 particles per image-substantially outperforming MP's 22.52% -- while also significantly suppressing axial period-jump errors. Experimental validation on nanoparticles confirms reliable single- and multi-particle localization throughout the entire working range. Our results establish ToW-PSFs as a powerful and practical optical encoding strategy for high-density, extended-range 3D localization imaging.
item.dc:creator: Lai Chen, Rui Wang, Li-Gang Wang

item.title: Intrinsic Orbital Nernst Effect in Real Photonic Bands
item.description: arXiv:2610.15621v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We predict an intrinsic orbital Nernst effect in reciprocal photonic lattices with real Bloch modes. In the collisionless regime, a thermal gradient generates a transverse angular-displacement response although band angular moments and ordinary Berry curvatures vanish. The response is carried by angular-density dipoles formed through virtual mixing of distinct spatial modes. Their correlation with band velocity survives thermal averaging and is independently recovered from the angular-density readout of unitarily evolved wave packets. Two controls expose the mechanism: a fixed-generator two-level system has zero antisymmetric intrinsic response, and flattening the dispersion suppresses transport without changing the eigenstates. A canonical scalar Maxwell calculation realizes the effect through symmetry-selected virtual channels, even when one band dominates the thermal population. These findings establish an orbital-dipole mechanism for intrinsic thermal angular transport in real photonic bands.
item.dc:creator: Tao Zhu

item.title: Nonperturbative optomechanics with thin, weakly reflective intracavity dielectrics
item.description: arXiv:2610.15749v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Levitated dielectric sensors are often treated as perturbative probes of a pre-existing optical field. We show that this picture fails for a novel sensor geometry: a dielectric plate whose transverse extent captures the full optical mode. Even an optically thin sensor with modest refractive index can heavily restructure the intracavity fields, effectively partitioning a cavity into two subcavities with substantial cross-coupling and producing new optical resonances and trapping sites with properties which deviate from the standard intuition. Conventional perturbative expressions for the cavity frequency shift and optomechanical coupling depart from the exact solution at thicknesses as small as $\sim\lambda/(10n)$. Furthermore, cavity locking decreases the coupling and increases the trap stiffness by orders of magnitude, and the coupled subcavity structure permits appreciable optical cooling at zero detuning, a distinct behavior unique to this nonperturbative regime. These effects, sharing a common origin, establish a distinct regime of cavity optomechanics in which the sensor is no longer merely a probe of the cavity field, but an element that helps define it.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Laeuger, Nancy Aggarwal

item.title: Direct growth of crack-free stoichiometric silicon nitride on sapphire for wide-band photonics
item.description: arXiv:2610.15754v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Low-loss stoichiometric silicon nitride on oxidized silicon has emerged as the major wide-band photonics platform for nonlinear and quantum photonics. These films, deposited by low-pressure chemical vapor deposition (LPCVD), are well known to have around 1000 MPa of residual tensile stress, which often leads to cracking when film thickness exceeds 400 nm. Although various stress-mitigation approaches can isolate or prevent cracking, this stress issue remains a major fabrication challenge. Low-residual-stress LPCVD stoichiometric silicon nitride on sapphire has also been reported and recently explored for photonics at telecommunication wavelengths. Here, we advance its development through systematic characterization, including thin-film stress analysis, ellipsometry and prism-coupling measurements of refractive index and loss, and swept-wavelength spectroscopy of fabricated photonic devices across a broad range of wavelengths. We demonstrate the direct growth of crack-free stoichiometric silicon nitride up to 2 {\mu}m thick with only 200 MPa of stress. Our fabricated devices show propagation losses of 0.35 dB/cm around 780 nm, 0.37 dB/cm around 1064 nm, and 0.25 dB/cm around 1630 nm. In addition, prism-coupling measurements indicate film losses below 1 dB/cm at wavelengths down to 500 nm. Our work highlights stoichiometric silicon nitride on sapphire as a promising wide-band photonics platform.

item.title: Photon-efficient readout of optical cavity arrays via spatial heterodyne
item.description: arXiv:2610.15827v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optical cavity arrays are an emerging tool for efficiently interfacing optical photons to quantum emitters for applications such as quantum computing. In this work, we demonstrate a metrology technique for such cavity arrays by interfering cavity array outputs against a tilted reference beam on a camera, constituting a spatial heterodyne. Both the amplitude and phase of each cavity's transmitted field can be extracted from the resulting images. Enabled by the improved scaling of heterodyne detection over intensity detection in the presence of technical noise, we demonstrate signal-to-noise ratio greater than one down to the single detected photon level, even in the presence of hundreds of noise equivalent photons. This readout technique holds promise for fast, non-destructive imaging of atomic qubits in cavity arrays by requiring fewer scattered photons while allowing the use of fast cameras with higher electronic readout noise.
item.dc:creator: Bridger McGimpsey, Matt Jaffe

item.title: Simultaneous Recovery of Dielectric Constants, Photoelastic Constants, and Strain Profiles from Picosecond Ultrasonic Echoes
item.description: arXiv:2610.15898v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Light reflected from a deforming solid depends on boundary motion and strain-induced modulation of the dielectric response. For a propagating acoustic field, scattering from different depths interferes coherently, so the measured optical amplitude and phase depend jointly on the strain profile, dielectric constant, and photoelastic constant. Optical tomography often makes such reconstructions tractable through independent projections. To probe mechanical strain, however, the optical measurement also depends on the material properties that mediate its observation, requiring those properties to be known or assumptions about the field. Here we show that broadband picosecond ultrasonic echoes in an opaque solid can supply the missing information. Fourier transformation of the measured complex relative reflectance change obtained with monochromatic light at normal incidence gives access to many acoustic frequency components. We recover the complex dielectric and photoelastic constants together with the nanoscale depth-dependent strain profile by formulating the reconstruction as a multiparameter nonlinear eigenvalue problem. We demonstrate the method using experimental echoes from a chromium film. The recovered refractive index agrees with ellipsometry, whereas the recovered strain profile closely follows a two-temperature-model prediction including electron and thermal diffusion and frequency-dependent ultrasonic attenuation. Synthetic echoes test robustness to added noise. Broadband response thus replaces additional optical projections, making the measurement self-calibrating and enabling simultaneous recovery of an unknown physical field and the material properties that mediate its optical observation.
item.dc:creator: Richard Wiltshaw, Motonobu Tomoda, Osamu Matsuda, Takehiro Tachizaki, Hirotsugu Ogi, Oliver B. Wright

item.title: Transfer learning-aided, artificial intelligence approach to evaluate optical properties of materials for classical and quantum photonic applications
item.description: arXiv:2610.15904v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this study, an artificial intelligence-assisted evaluation of the refractive indices of different materials is performed. The evaluation of the refractive index is necessary to design photonic devices for various classical and quantum photonic applications, and to theoretically analyse experimental results. The refractive index is one of the crucial parameters that affect the interaction of light with matter. Although the refractive index can be measured experimentally, its estimation via computational means provide the advantage of not requiring costly instrumentation, trained researchers and could avoid potential laboratory-based uncertainties. Therefore, in this study, artificial intelligence is implemented to estimate the optical constants of two types of materials, i.e., noble metals, and semiconductors. To this end, an artificial neural network is used to estimate the real and the imaginary parts of the refractive index of a specific material for various wavelengths of light. Then, the knowledge of the trained neural network is employed to initiate and train new neural networks to estimate the refractive indices of other materials. For the training of a neural network, various methods can be deployed. However, the application of the training can be a time-consuming process. A transfer learning approach is here implemented to provide a faster training solution for the problem under study. The implementation of transfer learning allows training the neural networks for a new material with higher speed or accuracy when compared to non-knowledge transfer-based training. Our results show the efficiency of the proposed technique in accurately evaluating the real and imaginary parts of the refractive index of different materials.
item.dc:creator: Mohammad Reza Habibi, Luca Sapienza, Juan C. Vasquez

item.title: Programmable spatiotemporal shaping for partially coherent structured wave packets
item.description: arXiv:2610.16254v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Providing more coherent light with space-time coupling offers unprecedented opportunities across diverse scientific disciplines and areas of technology. However, in many applications, tailored laser beams with partial coherence in space and time are desired. Here, we demonstrate a programmable approach for simultaneously shaping the intensity and coherence distributions of spatiotemporally coupled partially coherent wave packets. By jointly engineering the fractal speckle of a dynamic scatterer and applying tailored modulation of the illumination function, we experimentally generate partially coherent laser beams with arbitrarily designed intensity and nontrivial coherence distributions. The proposed approach is compatible with ultrafast laser pulses, enabling the on-demand generation of partially coherent space-time wave packets. The resulting spatiotemporally partially coherent wave packets exhibit non-separable space-time intensity profiles together with engineered spatiotemporal correlation distributions. This work provides a versatile framework for tailoring partially coherent light in space and time, with varied applications in relativistic laser-matter interaction, passive imaging and optical manipulation.
item.dc:creator: Zhao Zhang, Haihao Fan, Yaning Zhou, Weiran Li, Chaoliang Ding, Qiwen Zhan, Yangjian Cai, Xin Liu

item.title: High Sensitivity Transient Holographic Full-Polarization Microscopy
item.description: arXiv:2610.16370v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The polarization state of light provides direct access to ultrafast electronic, magnetic, and structural dynamics in materials. Transient wide-field microscopy with simultaneous amplitude, phase, and polarization sensitivity enables spatially resolved measurements of these dynamics, but its sensitivity is often limited by technical noise and background fluctuations. Here, we demonstrate transient holographic full-polarization microscopy with substantially reduced instrumental noise and sensitivity approaching the shot-noise limit. We compare holographic geometries using one, two, and four reference beams and find that the single-reference configuration provides the most favourable shot-noise-limited sensitivity for the derived polarization observables. Combined with two-camera detection, it simultaneously captures both orthogonal polarization components without distributing reference photons among multiple carriers. A self-referenced noise-reduction framework combining singular value decomposition and background subtraction further suppresses correlated noise. For spatially averaged regions, the baseline noise is reduced by factors of three-sixty, enabling detection of weaker transient responses at lower excitation densities and in weakly absorbing materials.
item.dc:creator: Julia A. Gessner, Philipp Kollenz, Godwin Maliyekkal, Milena R. Neubert, Garrett May, Lukas Becker, Nasrin Solhtalab, Tiago Buckup, Felix Deschler

item.title: Fading Memory and Nonlinear Dynamics in a Microring Resonator Network and their Use in Computation
item.description: arXiv:2610.16432v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Silicon microring resonators are promising components for photonic reservoir computing because their nonlinear optical response can transform signals and retain information about recent inputs. Under constant optical excitation, their coupled free-carrier and thermal dynamics can generate self-pulsing: a periodic output response. However, constant-input behavior does not reveal how these dynamics respond to randomly modulated signals or whether their memory is useful for temporal processing. Here, we characterize a single silicon microring resonator and a passive network of microring resonators under random input modulation. The temporal component associated with self-pulsing remains observable under random modulation, but the largest fading memory occurs near the self-pulsing boundary, where no resolved self-pulsing-like oscillation is present. reservoir computing metrics, such as memory capacity, map this accessible memory, and its decay provides effective timescales associated mainly with free-carrier and thermal relaxation. Finally, we use NARMA reconstruction to test whether the measured memory profile supports nonlinear temporal processing. Responses with a resolved self-pulsing-like component perform worse on this task, and the intrinsic memory profile is not matched to the required input history. These results show that reservoir computing metrics can characterize nonlinear microring resonator dynamics even when the physical system is not an effective standalone reservoir for the selected task.
item.dc:creator: Alessandro Foradori, Alessio Lugnan, Lorenzo Pavesi, Peter Bienstman

item.title: Asynchronous Terahertz-field sampling with soliton microcombs
item.description: arXiv:2610.16479v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Terahertz time-domain spectroscopy records the electric field of terahertz transients and underpins applications from materials science to non-destructive testing. Asynchronous optical sampling enables systems without moving parts, but its acquisition rate remains fundamentally limited by the repetition-rate of the driving femtosecond lasers. Here, we demonstrate asynchronous terahertz-field sampling with two chip-based soliton microcombs. Their ultrahigh 25 GHz pulse repetition-rate drastically reduces dead-time during acquisition, and stabilization via sideband injection-locking enables coherent averaging without active feedback loops. At 10 kHz acquisition rate, we achieve a dynamic range of 74 dB in a single 100 $\mu$s scan, and 100 dB after 50 ms of coherent averaging with a 1.6 THz bandwidth. Acquisition rates of up to 100 kHz are demonstrated, limited only by detection electronics. Together with a proof-of-concept silicon wafer thickness measurement, these results establish soliton microcombs as compact sources for rapid terahertz-field sampling.

item.title: Finite-event modulation transfer through forward-scattering media
item.description: arXiv:2610.16728v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How spatial structure is transferred through a forward-scattering medium depends jointly on pattern scale and propagation distance. Starting from photon exit displacements, we derive modulation transfer while retaining the number, depths, and projected angles of individual deflections, with event occurrences described by a homogeneous Poisson process along the propagation path. The second angular moment yields a leading low-frequency loss proportional to $k^2z^3$, where $k$ is angular spatial frequency and $z$ is thickness. At finite frequency, the model predicts two coupled departures: loss bends below its low-frequency quadratic extrapolation at fixed thickness, and transfer curves separate by thickness at fixed $k^2z^3$. The leading corrections to both effects arise from the same fourth angular moment. For symmetric, nondegenerate projected-angle distributions, the full response further establishes increasing loss with thickness in the same medium at fixed joint variable. Binary-pattern measurements through TiO$_2$ suspensions span five nominal loadings, seven thicknesses, and 20 spatial frequencies, supporting the approximate low-frequency scaling and showing both departures. A Gaussian effective-angle response calibrated only on lower-frequency data predicts the held-out higher-frequency band without refitting, with a logarithmic root-mean-square error of 0.0181 compared with 0.1021 for quadratic extrapolation. The results show that finite-event statistics provide a common physical origin for spectral bending and thickness-dependent departure from low-frequency scaling, linking coarse-pattern transport to finer spatial structure.
item.dc:creator: Chong Wang, Liangfeng Hu, Yuchen He, Huaibin Zheng, Hui Chen, Jianbin Liu, Yu Zhou, Zhuo Xu

item.title: Image Priors for Single-Shot Coded Diffraction Phase Retrieval
item.description: arXiv:2610.17064v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Phase retrieval recovers complex-valued objects from intensity-only measurements. In its classical Fourier form, reconstruction suffers from twin-image stagnation. Coded diffraction imaging, which adds a random phase mask before the Fourier transform, has so far required several masks. We show that an image prior makes single-shot coded diffraction imaging possible, with a single random mask followed by a Fourier transform. We validate this claim in simulation and in an optical experiment, in which a spatial light modulator displays the phase object together with the random mask. Our experimental validation covers five test signals and 530 images from the public Brno quantitative phase microscopy dataset of five adherent cell lines. With no image prior or with Fourier-only measurements, reconstruction of complex-valued objects from a single diffraction pattern consistently fails. An out-of-the-box pretrained image denoiser enables accurate reconstruction, in simulation even with fewer measurements than unknowns. Five regularization frameworks built on the same denoiser and one learned weakly convex regularizer all reconstruct the experimental images with peak signal-to-noise ratios within one decibel of each other. A single random phase mask and image priors thus turn coded diffraction imaging into a practical single-shot modality for quantitative phase imaging.
item.dc:creator: Zhiyuan Hu, YoonSeok Baek, Sylvain Gigan, Michael Unser, Jonathan Dong

item.title: Chiral Vector Beams for Topological Enantio-Sensitive Imaging
item.description: arXiv:2610.17111v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Molecular chiral discrimination is vital across chemistry and life sciences, yet optical approaches remain highly inefficient for small organic molecules. Here we turn vector beams, whose polarization carries a topological charge, into an efficient probe of molecular handedness. We show that the combination of a tightly focused radially polarized beam at the fundamental frequency {\omega} and an azimuthally polarized beam at 2{\omega} creates chiral vector beams, a locally chiral field with structured handedness. Using state-of-the-art computational modeling in the chiral molecule carvone, we show that the nonlinear response (notably sum-frequency generation) of randomly oriented chiral molecules to this chiral vector beam captures the fields' local handedness and is highly enantio-sensitive. The two enantiomers emit light at frequency 3{\omega} with topological ring structures of different divergence, and thus the molecular handedness can be read out directly from the ring radius. The signal inherits the Poincar\'e index of the driving field, opening up new ways to robust, ultrafast, and and all-optical chiral discrimination.

item.title: Programmable Hard-X-Ray Spectral Comb Generation via Laser-Compton Scattering
item.description: arXiv:2610.17166v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Independent control of line spacing and offset underpins programmable frequency-comb spectroscopy, yet it has not been established for hard-X-ray sources based on inverse Compton scattering after electron transport and angular collection. Self-consistent multi-particle tracking and Li'enard-Wiechert radiation calculations model a transported 10 pC beam and its angle-integrated spectrum near 11 keV. Laser pulse separation programs the comb spacing, while pulse-to-pulse phase translates the entire line grid at fixed spacing. The spacing model agrees within 0.52%, while transport and optics change the phase-transfer slope by less than 0.2%. At fixed electron spot size, the largest resolvable separation scales as the inverse square of normalized emittance; subnanometer bunches also produce a mode-locked train with 13.9 as spacing. This two-coordinate programmability enables phase-stepped multicolor measurements and offers routes to hard-X-ray Ramsey interferometry, coherent control of core and nuclear excitations, and attosecond nonlinear spectroscopy.
item.dc:creator: Hao Zhang, 1Ji Qiang, Shukui Zhang, Sergio Carbajo

item.title: Observation of Photon Bunching in Broadband Multimode Thermal Light Enabled by Temporal Imaging
item.description: arXiv:2610.17228v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Photons emitted by incoherent sources exhibit temporal bunching, a fundamental manifestation of Bose-Einstein statistics first observed by Hanbury Brown and Twiss (HBT). While intensity correlation measurements originated in astronomy and are now central across quantum technologies, biophysics, and spectroscopy, observing temporal bunching in broadband thermal light remains limited by detector temporal resolution. Conventional approaches - such as streak cameras or optical upconversion - introduce severe trade-offs in efficiency, bandwidth, or setup versatility. Here, we propose and demonstrate a third route: pre-detection temporal magnification of the optical field prior to measuring its intensity autocorrelation function in a conventional HBT setup. Using an electro-optic time lens with a temporal magnification of 660, we resolve the temporal intensity autocorrelation of broadband thermal light generated via non-degenerate spontaneous parametric down-conversion with a bandwidth of 250 GHz. This enables direct observation of thermal photon bunching on sub-3.5 picosecond timescales without narrow spectral filtering, establishing pre-detection temporal imaging as a general platform for broadband statistical optics, with applications spanning ultrafast quantum optics, biophysical imaging, and potentially stellar intensity interferometry.
item.dc:creator: Filip So\'snicki, Micha{\l} Miko{\l}ajczyk, Sanjay Kapoor, Dmitri B. Horoshko, Mikhail I. Kolobov, Micha{\l} Karpi\'nski

item.title: Zeptosecond-level timing-noise floor in optical-to-terahertz photomixing
item.description: arXiv:2610.17364v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optical generation of terahertz (0.1 to 10\,THz) carriers can, in principle, preserve the spectral purity of an optical reference without the noise penalty associated with electronic frequency multiplication. Here, we identify and suppress the dominant excess-noise mechanisms that limit this conversion in high-power uni-travelling-carrier photodiodes. We characterize amplitude-to-phase conversion as functions of photocurrent and reverse bias and identify operating parameters to minimize the effect. We quantify the white phase noise introduced by optical amplification and show that this contribution can be eliminated by directly driving the photodiode with a high-power optical source. With the excess noise mitigated, we use cross-correlation phase-noise measurements to observe a white phase-noise floor of $-161.0$~dBc/Hz at 263.2~GHz, corresponding to a timing-noise floor of 7.6~zs/$\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}$. The remaining floor follows the photocurrent dependence expected from shot noise. Extending the measurement across the full WR-3.4 band, from 220 to 330~GHz, yields timing-noise floors below 10~zs/$\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}$ throughout, with a minimum of 6.0~zs/$\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}$. These results establish direct photomixing as a route to sub-10-zs/$\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}$ white timing-noise floors for continuous-wave sources at terahertz frequencies and identify the noise processes that must be controlled to reach this regime.
item.dc:creator: William F. McGrew, James Greenberg, Scott C. Egbert, Brendan M. Heffernan, Y. Lange Simmons, Tatsuya Tanigawa, Kazutoshi Kato, Tadao Nagatsuma, Antoine Rolland

item.title: Non-contact lens metrology from optical flow and differentiable ray tracing
item.description: arXiv:2610.17515v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate lens surface metrology is essential to determine the manufactured geometry of refractive optical elements and their deviation from the specified design. We demonstrate a transmission metrology method that reconstructs refractive lens surfaces from the displacement of a wavelet-noise-patterned mask. Lens-induced distortion is represented by a dense displacement field. A differentiable ray tracer fits the lens geometry using a calibrated near-telecentric camera model with an effective finite ray origin. We validate the method on commercial lenses. The recovered geometries agree with nominal specifications, and the plano-aspheric reconstruction is compared with chromatic confocal profilometry.
item.dc:creator: Hector A. Jimenez-Romero, Wolfgang Heidrich

item.title: Inverse design of poles and zeros: tailoring phase control in metasurfaces
item.description: arXiv:2610.17587v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a physically interpretable inverse-design framework for generalized Huygens metasurfaces, using prescribed scattering poles and zeros to engineer resonance interference and transmission-phase control. Compared with direct optimization of transmission or reflection coefficients, this approach offers a physically transparent route to rationally controlling resonance properties, including linewidth and group delay, while reducing computational cost. The resulting designs demonstrate how near-unity transmission and $2\pi$ phase excursion can arise from resonance interference. These signatures of the Kerker effect extend beyond the conventional alignment of electric and magnetic dipole resonances to other mechanisms, including guided-mode resonances and quasi-bound states in the continuum. We further optimize the Kerker condition across a continuum of refractive-index states in a reconfigurable phase change material metasurface, enabling high-transmission $2\pi$ phase tuning. Our results establish a versatile and practical approach to metasurface phase control through the targeted design of scattering poles and zeros.
item.dc:creator: Junhe Zhang, Seoyoung Kim, Hyun Jung Kim, Juejun Hu

item.title: Practical Mid-infrared Dual-comb Spectroscopy with Absolute Frequency Referencing Based on a Single-cavity Dual-comb Fiber Laser
item.description: arXiv:2610.17822v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We demonstrate a practical mid-infrared (MIR) dual-comb spectroscopy (DCS) method based on a bidirectional dual-comb fiber laser. By exploiting the inherently high relative stability and mutual coherence of the dual-comb laser, we stabilize the MIR dual-comb modes with sufficient precision using only piezoelectric control of the repetition frequencies. This simple configuration enables correction of residual timing jitter and phase noise in interferograms while preserving the absolute optical frequency scale defined by the experimentally obtained comb parameters, without requiring an external continuous-wave laser reference or tight phase-locking. Importantly, the proposed method does not merely produce apparently clean interferograms through signal processing, but enables coherent averaging while retaining both the physically meaningful interferometric waveforms and well-defined absolute frequency information. The proposed system is experimentally validated through MIR spectroscopy of N$_2$O around 3.9 $\mu$m, achieving a signal-to-noise ratio of approximately 690 through coherent averaging of 10,000 interferograms over 65 s, along with the acquisition of an absorption spectrum consistent with the reference data. These results demonstrate a simple and practical approach to absolute-frequency-referenced MIR-DCS.
item.dc:creator: Akifumi Asahara, Kaoru Minoshima

item.title: Theory of deeply subwavelength electromagnetic structuring of semiconductors due to thermal-ionization instability
item.description: arXiv:2610.17847v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a theory of ionization-assisted instability that governs the reflection of intense electromagnetic pulses from a semiconductor surface. Local overheating of the material increases the free-carrier density and conductivity, which in turn enhances the absorption of the incident radiation and further amplifies local heating and avalanche ionization. At high pump repetition rates, the overheating accumulates from pulse to pulse, leading to a gradual rise of the local material temperature and free carrier density - a positive feedback loop that drives thermal runaway. However, this effect competes with diffraction of the pump field on the emerging perturbation of the dielectric permittivity or on the surface relief, which reduces the local electric field amplitude in the overheated regions, thus providing negative feedback. We show that the competition between heat diffusion and diffraction near-field weakening creates conditions for the exponential growth of temperature perturbations with a certain wavenumber determined by the pulse repetition rate, pump field, thermal conductivity and other material parameters. The derived analytical expressions accurately describe the spatial period of deeply subwavelength structures observed in recent experiments on silicon structuring by intense terahertz radiation, and reproduce qualitatively dependencies of their period on the pump intensity, the incident wavelength and the number of pump pulses.
item.dc:creator: I. V. Oladyshkin, D. I. Kulshin, E. O. Smolina

item.title: On-chip optical isolators
item.description: arXiv:2610.17862v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optical isolation suppresses back-reflections that destabilize lasers, produce parasitic interference, and increase crosstalk in photonic systems. Although free-space and fibre-optic isolators are mature, no broadly adopted on-chip technology yet combines strong isolation, low insertion loss, broad bandwidth, compact footprint, and scalable fabrication. The difficulty is twofold: Lorentz reciprocity must be broken, and every relevant backward spatial, spectral, and polarization channel must be suppressed. This Review develops a common framework for assessing proposed solutions. We first distinguish pairwise nonreciprocity from intensity-asymmetric transmission and from true isolation using the constitutive relations and scattering matrix. We then compare three physical routes to an integrated nonreciprocal response: magneto-optical bias, externally driven space-time modulation, and nonlinear optical processes. Topological and non-Hermitian systems are treated as cross-cutting design frameworks that can route, protect, or enhance an underlying nonreciprocal response, but do not by themselves break reciprocity. Finally, we examine fundamental constraints and practical trade-offs among isolation, insertion loss, bandwidth, footprint, modal coverage, drive requirements, and fabrication compatibility. The resulting mechanism-based perspective connects reciprocity-breaking physics to the requirements of scalable photonic integrated circuits.
item.dc:creator: Abanoub Mikhail, Nikolay Solodovchenko, Sen Xu, Fan Zhang, Maksim Tumashov, Mingzhao Song, Sergei Makarov, Andrey Bogdanov

item.title: A Photonic Integrated Light Generation, Control, and Delivery Engine for Creating Cold Atoms
item.description: arXiv:2610.17918v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The creation of cold atoms underpins quantum sensing and precision metrology, computing, timekeeping, and fundamental science experiments. Miniaturizing the lasers and optical infrastructure, which occupy over 80% of the volume of these experiments, through photonic integration could improve robustness, reliability, and manufacturability while reducing cost and enabling portable space-based precision measurements and quantum tools for non-experts. Yet, there has been limited progress towards integration of the laser and optical infrastructure required to generate cold atoms onto a single chip. We demonstrate a photonic engine that generates, controls, and delivers precision light to create cold atoms in a rubidium 3-dimensional magneto-optical trap (3D-MOT). We integrate on a single chip two frequency-agile self-injection-locked lasers, laser frequency and intensity control, passive beam combining and splitting, signal monitoring, and high-efficiency beam delivery to a rubidium vapor cell. The integrated engine is shown to support multiple functions required for generating cold atoms including stable generation of low-noise cooling and repump light, frequency control for atom spectroscopy and stabilization, real-time laser monitoring, routing for laser offset locking, optical power modulation, and large-area three-beam delivery of 3 mW to the physics package. Fully electrically controlled, the engine enables sustained 3D-MOT operation, trapping more than 1 million atoms at an average temperature of 350 uK and supporting atom-number and temperature measurements. These results demonstrate the first single-chip integration of light generation, control, and delivery for cold-atom generation, offering a path toward smaller, more robust, and manufacturable cold-atom systems for applications including cold-atom clocks and sensors.
item.dc:creator: Andrei Isichenko, Calisto Ruiz, Chuan Zhong, Nick Montifiore, Sam J. Harding, Meiting Song, Chenghang Liu, Nitin Indukuri, Karl D. Nelson, Daniel J. Blumenthal

item.title: Recovery-Oriented Optical System Design Based on Fisher Information
item.description: arXiv:2610.17950v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Traditional optical system design for imaging applications has long been guided by image quality metrics such as geometrical RMS spot size, wavefront error, and modulation transfer function (MTF). Although these metrics effectively characterize direct imaging performance, they do not necessarily indicate optimal behavior when image restoration is subsequently applied. In modern imaging pipelines, however, optical systems are increasingly combined with physics-based or learning-based restoration methods, making the information transfer properties of the optical system critically important. In this work, we propose a recovery-oriented optical design approach that explicitly links optical system optimization with image restoration performance through an estimation-theoretic framework based on Fisher information. A new design criterion is adopted to ensure that the information encoded by the optical system can be reliably recovered during image restoration. To validate the proposed approach, two dual separated aspheric lenses are designed under identical configurations using conventional RMS-based optimization and the proposed recovery-oriented optimization, respectively. Although the RMS-optimized lens exhibits superior direct imaging quality, it underperforms after image restoration compared to the recovery-oriented design. These results demonstrate that recovery-oriented optical design provides a physically interpretable and effective extension of traditional optical design criteria for imaging systems operating within modern computational imaging pipelines.
item.dc:creator: Zhuang Qian, Yan Mo, Hao Tan, Yu Chen, Haibo Wang, Weining Guo, Yijie Ni, Donglin Ma

item.title: Imaging the building blocks of ant pheromone communication
item.description: arXiv:2610.18079v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Organisms have evolved diverse strategies to communicate. Beyond acoustic and visual signals, many species rely on chemical communication, including pheromones: volatile compounds involved in reproduction, defense, and coordination. Ant trail systems, a paradigm of pheromone use, have inspired decades of research in collective behavior, self-organization and optimization algorithms. Yet, despite their central role, individual pheromone deposits have never been directly visualized or quantified, limiting our understanding of how deposition events scale into collective trail formation. Here, we use interferometric imaging to reveal and quantify single pheromone deposits in the ant Lasius niger. This label-free, non-invasive approach enables precise measurement of single deposit volume (~1 pL, with x20-fold variability), morphology, and temporal dynamics. We uncover a two-phase volume loss process: most of secreted volume evaporates within seconds, forming a dried droplet, which then partially sublimates (~10%) over one hour. These findings challenge the assumption of homogeneous deposition and bring previously inaccessible properties of ant pheromone trails within experimental reach. Our method establishes a quantitative framework for studying the spatiotemporal dynamics of insect chemical communication, linking individual signaling to collective patterns.

item.title: Chirality Inversion and Giant Optical Activity in Scalable Self-Assembled Metamaterials
item.description: arXiv:2610.18116v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Chiral materials manipulate light in ways that hold promise for sensing, imaging, and photonics, but producing such materials with strong and reproducible optical activity at large scale remains challenging. Here, we develop a scalable strategy to assemble hierarchical helicoidal metamaterials from metallic nanoparticles and chitin nanocrystals, a biosourced polysaccharide. Spontaneous co-assembly produces ordered chiral structures with strong plasmonic optical activity, reaching a dissymmetry factor of 0.55. The unprecedented ability to vary the helicoidal pitch allows control of the optical response, enabling inversion of optical handedness without changing the handedness of the template, effectively decoupling geometrical chirality from optical chirality. Remarkably, the gold nanoparticles can also be recovered from dry films and redispersed as colloids, introducing an appealing circularity concept for sustainable chiral plasmonic materials.

item.title: Experimental Demonstration of 7-Dimensional N-Vector Model with Dimensional Inflation and Annealing
item.description: arXiv:2610.18153v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We report the first experimental realization of a physical system described by a high-dimensional Hamiltonian comprising up to seven dimensions. Our setup is based on a holographic optical computer, which realizes a dimensional inflation by spatial and temporal multiplexing of lower dimensional systems. We demonstrate an $N$-vector model, with applications in field theory and computing. The approach is scalable and enables table-top implementation of high-dimensional theoretical models, and novel methods for combinatorial optimization. We experimentally demonstrate dimensional annealing: by dynamically reducing the number of dimensions, the ground state of an Ising model is found in complex graphs by an adiabatic evolution from high-dimensional spaces.
item.dc:creator: Daniele Veraldi, Marcello Calvanese Strinati, Paolo Charlesworth, Matteo Spaziani, Silvia Gentilini, Davide Pierangeli, Claudio Conti

item.title: Feedback-Controlled Self-Trapping of Solitons
item.description: arXiv:2610.18191v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Chip-scale microresonator-based frequency combs, commonly referred to as microcombs, are promising sources for field-deployable metrology applications. However, intrinsic microresonator noise can make it difficult to generate microcombs with sufficiently low noise for applications. A widely used approach to overcome this limitation is to trap the DKS in the microresonator by phase-modulating the pump laser, although integrating a low-noise modulation reference in a fully on-chip platform remains challenging. Here, we propose an optoelectronic self-trapping scheme in which the impact of intrinsic microresonator noise on microcomb repetition-rate jitter is suppressed through feedback-controlled phase modulation of the driving laser so that the intrinsic noise of the laser sets the ultimate performance limit. This modification eliminates the need for an external low-phase-noise RF source, thereby enabling chip integration. We develop both analytical and numerical models for the proposed system and benchmark its performance against conventional externally referenced bulk implementations, showing that the proposed approach achieves comparable microcomb noise suppression while maintaining chip-scale compatibility.
item.dc:creator: Raonaqul Islam, Pradyoth Shandilya, Yunxiang Song, Alioune Niang, Gary Carter, Thomas Carruthers, Curtis Menyuk, Ergun Simsek

item.title: Optical parametric amplification of spatiotemporal optical vortices
item.description: arXiv:2610.18203v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spatiotemporal optical vortices (STOVs) are structured light featuring a phase singularity in the spatiotemporal domain, exhibiting unique topology that couples spatial and temporal dimensions. To date, amplification of STOVs remains unexplored, and their wavelength tunability is limited by available light sources. In this work, we present the theoretical analysis and experimental demonstration of optical parametric amplification (OPA) of STOVs. The pulse energy of the STOV signal is enhanced by a factor of 60, while its spatiotemporal structure is robustly preserved. The generated idler inherits the phase-conjugated STOV topology with the opposite topological charge, governed by simultaneous conservation of energy, linear momentum, and spatiotemporal orbital angular momentum. The intrinsic wavelength-conversion capability of OPA further provides a route towards spectrally tunable STOV generation, spanning from visible to near-infrared wavelength regimes. This work paves the way toward further development of multi-stage amplification architectures, facilitating applications of wavelength-tunable spatiotemporally structured light at ultrahigh intensities.
item.dc:creator: Houan Teng, Chenhao Wan, Qiwen Zhan

item.title: Orbital Angular Momentum Transfer and Beam-Quality Limits in Fork-Grating Electron Diffraction
item.description: arXiv:2610.18401v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We analyze fork-grating generation of electron vortex beams beyond the ideal single-mode approximation. The incident beam is described as a paraxial Gaussian ensemble with finite transverse momentum spread and a first electromagnetic Hartree phase accumulated before the grating. Within Fresnel propagation we derive an analytical expression for each diffraction order and determine the corresponding orbital-angular-momentum statistics. The mean OAM of a selected order remains fixed by the topological rule, $\langle L_z\rangle_m=mp\hbar$, while its variance is set by the residual transverse momentum spread of the beam prepared at the grating. For the Gaussian mixture, the transverse purity is $\mathcal P_{\perp,m}=[1+2(\Delta L_{z,m}/\hbar)^2]^{-1}$. The observed annular profile is governed by a separate propagation-dependent blurring scale, so a beam can retain well-defined mean OAM while having low transverse purity or a partially filled vortex minimum. Within the radial phase-screen approximation, the Hartree self-field modifies the propagated profile while preserving the full-plane OAM moments and transverse purity.
item.dc:creator: P. K. Tsiopa, S. S. Baturin

item.title: Continuous-wave 148.4-nm generation in strontium tetraborate for nuclear absorption spectroscopy
item.description: arXiv:2610.18470v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Continuous-wave light near 148.4 nm enables direct absorption spectroscopy of the thorium-229 nuclear transition. We demonstrate single-pass frequency doubling in strontium tetraborate, delivering an estimated 8.1 nW at 920 mW pump power. At this power, oxygen admission leaves a background of 1.22 kHz, corresponding to an estimated signal-to-background ratio of 3.8 x 10^4 after current-integration calibration. Several crystals grown by top-seeded solution growth produce polarization-dependent VUV signals. Temperature scans reveal distinct maxima among specimens cut from one boule and among positions within a specimen. The source sustains operation over 33.3 h. In a separate 3-h record acquired with 1-ms gates, local referencing achieves near-Poisson averaging, reaching a fractional Allan deviation of 3.5 x 10^-5 at 1000 s. These results establish a practical VUV source for stable, long-duration spectroscopy of weak nuclear absorption.
