item.title: Continuous-wave 148.4 nm Generation in Quasi-phase Matched BaMgF4
item.description: arXiv:2610.18519v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We report continuous-wave (CW) vacuum-ultraviolet (VUV) generation at 148.4 nm by second-harmonic generation of 296.8-nm fundamental light in quasi-phase matched (QPM) BaMgF4 (BMF). At the incident power of 170 mW, a VUV output power of approximately 31 pW can be obtained. The quadratic dependence of the signal on the incident power in the QPM region and its attenuation in the ambient environment support the identification of VUV generation. The polarization dependence shows a sine-function shape with a 15% output attenuation from the maximum to the minimum. These results highlight the potential of BMF as a nonlinear medium for CW VUV generation.
item.dc:creator: Yuanzhuang Bu, Xiangting Wang, Ruiyin Gu, Chongtai Liu, Luxin Jiang, Xinqing Ding, Ke Zhang, Yongkai Li, Kemi Xu

item.title: Mode locking by phase-sensitive amplification
item.description: arXiv:2610.18559v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mode locking is the mechanism by which lasers organize many optical modes into stable trains of ultrashort pulses. It underpins optical frequency combs, precision timing and spectroscopy, and provides the phase-coherent waveforms required for applications ranging from strong-field physics to optical frequency metrology. Conventional pulse-forming mechanisms select pulse amplitude without fixing its phase relative to an external optical reference, leaving pulse formation and optical-phase stabilization as separate functions. Phase-sensitive amplification offers a different possibility: the optical reference can participate directly in pulse formation. Here we demonstrate this principle in a continuously pumped oscillator. Kerr-induced phase evolution and cavity detuning turn pump-referenced parametric gain into a power-dependent discriminator that supports stable single-soliton operation. Roundtrip-resolved interferometry reveals that the soliton optical phase remains referenced to the master laser modulo $\pi$. These results establish phase-sensitive mode locking, in which pulse-amplitude selection and optical-phase referencing arise from the same coherent nonlinear feedback.
item.dc:creator: Francesco De Lucia, Yifan Sun, Georges Semaan, Clement Dupont, Nicolas Englebert, Simon-Pierre Gorza, Fran\c{c}ois Leo

item.title: Probing topological edge states in multilayer dielectric photonic nanostructures
item.description: arXiv:2610.18700v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Topological photonics has recently attracted a significant attention, leading to many theoretical studies and predictions. However, direct experimental demonstrations of topology-driven effects, particularly in nanostructures, are rarely proven. In this work, we experimentally investigate multilayer photonic nanostructures composed of alternating subwavelength dielectric layers, arranged according to the topological Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. By engineering different edge truncations, we probe different supported topological phases. Our theoretical predictions and experimental measurements reveal strong field confinement at the surface exclusively in the configuration supporting topological edge states, providing their localized character and topological origin. First, we demonstrate enhanced absorption in an ultrathin absorbing overlayer deposited on the surface when the topological surface mode is present, highlighting the potential for surface-sensing applications. Second, we observe enhanced second-harmonic generation in reflection from the surface, demonstrating the potential of topological states for surface enhanced nonlinear optics enabled by the strong localization of the electromagnetic field at the interface.
item.dc:creator: Eva Otero, Ivan Toftul, Michael Scalora, Jose Trull, Crina Cojocaru, Yuri Kivshar

item.title: Engineering Color and Angular Stability in Building-Integrated Photovoltaics Using Metal-Oxide Photonic Glasses
item.description: arXiv:2610.18759v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coloring building-integrated photovoltaics poses a dilemma: absorptive pigments cost photocurrent, while ordered photonic structures are iridescent. Amorphous photonic glasses, disordered packings of high-index nanospheres, are proposed to avoid both, yet their angle-independent color has rarely been quantified on a realistic module stack. A non-absorbing scatterer needs a high index with visible transparency, which the Moss rule caps near 2.35. Coupling Mie scattering, the Percus-Yevick structure factor, the exact phase function, and two-flux transfer with absorption and refraction at the front glass, we fix four target colors that a crowd-sourced naming survey calls unambiguously blue, green, gold, and terracotta, and map the recipes reaching them across four metal oxides, four encapsulants, two cell technologies, and wide ranges of particle size, packing fraction, and layer number. All four are reached in a laminated three-layer coating, to within DeltaE00 of 0.8 to 2.5, but not from one oxide: transparent TiO2 renders the blue and only pale warm tones; the green, gold, and terracotta require the blue-band absorption of V2O5, and the low-contrast oxides turn grey at the warm end. The encapsulant governs the color, and the cell technology does not. Disorder does not confer angle independence: the colors hold for an observer moving under a fixed sun but drift by DeltaE00 of 5 to 18 over the day, terracotta least, and a facade lit from above and viewed from below shifts every color towards the blue. Oxide, layer number, and facade geometry must therefore be designed together.
item.dc:creator: Sinan Genc, Talat Ozden, Alpan Bek

item.title: Domain of Applicability of the Distorted Wave Born Approximation (DWBA): A Critical Analysis for X-ray and Visible-Light Interface Scattering
item.description: arXiv:2610.14054v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Distorted Wave Born Approximation (DWBA) is established for X-ray interface scattering, yet its domain of applicability has never been stated explicitly. The DWBA implicitly rests on the small refractive index deviation (SRID) condition - satisfied by X-rays ($|n-1| \sim 10^{-6}$) but violated by visible light ($|n-1| \sim 0.5$). The DWBA mixes microscopic and macroscopic Maxwell equations, whereas a rigorous optical theory must be built on the macroscopic Maxwell equations and constitutive relations. Rigorous alternatives for two specific inconsistencies in the standard DWBA are discussed. The Extended Transfer Matrix Approach (ETMA) for visible-light interface scattering is outlined.
item.dc:creator: Reinhard Sigel

item.title: Precursor stoichiometry controls dopant structure, defect chemistry, and valence in Mn-doped ZnGa$_2$O$_4$ nanocrystals
item.description: arXiv:2610.14195v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The luminescence of doped nanocrystals is usually optimised through the activator; here we show that the host cation ratio is an equally decisive, and largely overlooked, design variable. Mn-doped ZnGa$_2$O$_4$ nanocrystals (Mn:Zn = $4\times10^{-4}$) were grown hydrothermally at nominal Zn/Ga ratios between 0.30 and 0.75 (stoichiometric: 0.50) and post-annealed at 400--1100$^\circ$C, and the resulting composition--temperature matrix was mapped by X-ray- and UV-excited luminescence, EPR, Rietveld-refined X-ray diffraction, Raman spectroscopy and SEM. The as-grown crystals are phase-pure spinel at every composition and accommodate their off-stoichiometry internally as a point-defect inventory, reflected in a 0.4\% variation of the lattice parameter; on annealing, the excess gallium is exsolved as $\beta$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ in amounts set by the solution composition. The Mn$^{2+}$ emission separates into two optima, near-stoichiometric crystals annealed at 400--600$^\circ$C and Zn-excess crystals annealed at 1100$^\circ$C, the latter being twice as bright under X-ray excitation. Under X-ray and 365~nm excitation the two optima are separated by a minimum at 800$^\circ$C that coincides with a collapse of the Mn$^{2+}$ EPR population and has no counterpart in the Raman linewidths, identifying transient, defect-compensated oxidation of the dopant rather than lattice degradation as its origin. The most Zn-rich composition shows neither Mn$^{2+}$ nor Mn$^{4+}$ emission at any annealing stage, whereas its trace Cr$^{3+}$ emission is strong, indicating that Mn is rejected already during growth. Solution stoichiometry therefore acts on two levels, dopant capture and native-defect inventory, while annealing controls dopant valence and lattice order. The brightest high-temperature phosphor is thus not the nominally stoichiometric one, but the composition whose excess is consumed on its way to stoichiometry.
item.dc:creator: M\'aty\'as M. Rudolf, G\'abor Bortel, Nikoletta Jegeny\'es, \'Arp\'ad Jakab, L\'aszl\'o Bencs, Ferenc Simon, Adam Gali, D\'avid Beke

item.title: Interpretation of chirality imprinted on photoelectron momentum spectra by three-dimensional light fields
item.description: arXiv:2610.14557v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Synthetic three-dimensional (3D) light fields provide a new route to imprinting chirality on achiral matter through light--matter interaction. Although previous work has numerically demonstrated that chirality can be imprinted on the photoelectron momentum spectrum of atoms, a transparent analytical physical picture that links the structure of the driving field to the chirality of the spectrum is still an open question. Here, using frequency-domain theory based on nonperturbative quantum electrodynamics (QED), we demonstrate that this chirality originates from coherence between adjacent quantum transition channels. We further find that a symmetry transformation introduces into the coherence term a symmetry-breaking phase shift ($\Phi_{\mathrm{SBPS}}$), which can be tuned by varying the laser-field parameters to preserve or break the corresponding symmetry in the spectrum. Once all such symmetries are broken, the momentum spectrum becomes chiral. In particular, for the noncollinear two-color 3D light field considered here, the spectrum is chiral for even $f=\omega_2/\omega_1$ and achiral for odd $f$. Our results provide a microscopic interpretation of chirality imprinting and establish a framework for predicting and controlling chiral electron wave packets with synthetic 3D light fields.
item.dc:creator: Junxin Yuan, Yuhong Li, Fei Li, Jinkai Zhang, Shiyang Zhong, Hao Teng, Yujun Yang, Yingchun Guo, Zhiyi Wei, Jing Chen, Xiaojun Liu, Bingbing Wang

item.title: Stackelberg Game with Multi-Agent Transformer for ISRS-Aware Resource Re-optimization in Multi-Band Optical Networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.14830v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The rapid expansion of generative AI is driving computing infrastructures toward interconnected AI data centers. Multi-band optical networks have become the backbone of such connectivity. To accommodate increasingly dynamic traffic demands, these networks require continual resource re-optimization to improve resource utilization and reduce service blocking. However, multi-band transmission amplifies inter-channel stimulated Raman scattering(ISRS), inducing nonlinear coupling among services. This coupling complicates re-optimization, as local adjustments perturb the global power profile, creating interdependent optimization decisions across services. Moreover, the nonlinear interactions vary with the subset of services selected for re-optimization, and inappropriate selection may reduce re-optimization effectiveness or diminish achievable benefits. To address these challenges, we propose a Stackelberg Game with Multi-Agent Transformer (SG-MAT) approach for ISRS-aware resource re-optimization. SG-MAT employs a leader-follower structure, in which the MAT-based follower models nonlinear coupling and generates coordinated channel reallocations, feeding the utilization improvements to the leader. Using this feedback, the leader identifies critical service subsets, approximating a Stackelberg equilibrium to guide global decisions and enabling consistent and efficient re-optimization. Simulation results show that SG-MAT achieves the highest utilization improvement and reduces the blocking ratio by approximately 30% under moderate traffic loads, with computational complexity comparable to benchmarks.
item.dc:creator: Jiaxin Liu, Rentao Gu, Miao Zhu, Zeguang Zou, Hui Li, Yuefeng Ji

item.title: Partial-coherence weak measurement of polarization qubits with a temporal pointer: theory and experiment
item.description: arXiv:2610.14954v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Weak measurement has proven useful for metrology, for probing quantum paradoxes, and for the direct measurement of quantum states. Weak measurements of polarization qubits with temporal pointers provide a direct route to weak-value characterization, including in regimes where the pointer is only partially coherent. We derive a closed-form expression for the post-selected temporal shift that interpolates between the incoherent and coherent (ideal) weak-measurement limits through a single parameter $\nu$, the pointer visibility. The expression is experimentally tested for a range of polarization states spanning three trajectories corresponding to rotations about the principal axes of the Poincar\'e sphere. Two of the trajectories provide parameter-free benchmarks, with the real part of the weak value following $\cos^2\theta$ and $1/2$. In contrast, the weak value along the third trajectory is sensitive to incoherence and is well described by the single-parameter partial-coherence model, from which a reduced pointer visibility is obtained. Time shifts are extracted from the smoothed derivative of the pulse leading edge with internal calibration, reaching few-picosecond precision on 10 ns optical pulses using commercial components. The same apparatus also gives qualitative access to the imaginary quadrature through the frequency centroid, showing that temporal weak measurements remain accessible and quantitative in partially coherent pulsed systems.
item.dc:creator: Shane P. Gervais, Lambert Giner

item.title: Interfacial Coupling Reshapes Nonlinear Polarization in a Spin-Defect van der Waals Heterostructure
item.description: arXiv:2610.15189v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Van der Waals heterostructures offer a direct route to couple an optically active layer to a two-dimensional spin sensor, yet their coherent nonlinear response at interfaces remains poorly resolved. Here, we use polarization-resolved second harmonic-generation imaging to resolve four distinct regions of a hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) -based heterostructure, native hBN, neutron-irradiated hBN containing negatively charged boron vacancies (VB-), PbI2 and their complete overlap. The detected intensity scales quadratically with incident power, consistent with a dominant second-order optical process. Polarization scans show that adding PbI2 transforms the distorted VB- SHG anisotropy into a predominantly fourfold response with a sixfold stronger SHG than native hBN alone. This non-additive nonlinear response occurs in the same layer architecture also shown to enhance defect photoluminescence, linking spin-defect sensitization to an interface-modified effective second-order susceptibility.
item.dc:creator: Lena Dalifoski, Eveline Mayner, Poonam Singh

item.title: Monogamy of quantum steering in exciton--cavity optomechanical system
item.description: arXiv:2610.15233v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this work, we study a theoretical scheme to investigate the monogamy of quantum steering in a hybrid exciton--cavity optomechanical (EOM) system. Within the Gaussian-state formalism, we quantify the steerability among the exciton, photon, and mechanical modes in both the steady-state and dynamical regimes. We establish and verify CKW-type monogamy inequalities for Gaussian steering and demonstrate that the distribution of bipartite steering among the three modes can be controlled through the system parameters. We further examine the influence of thermal noise and temporal evolution on the steering properties and the corresponding monogamy relations. Our results show that increasing the temperature generally suppresses the strength of Gaussian steering and modifies the degree of steering sharing imposed by the CKW-type monogamy relations. In contrast, in the dynamical regime, the steerability can increase with evolution time over suitable temporal windows, indicating that the transient dynamics can be exploited to enhance quantum correlations. These results highlight the potential of hybrid exciton--optomechanical platforms for controllable quantum correlations and provide a promising route toward the generation and manipulation of multipartite quantum resources.
item.dc:creator: Hamza Harraf, Mohamed Amazioug, Rachid Ahl Laamara

item.title: Three-dimensional reconstruction of weakly scattering objects from single-defocus 4D-STEM data
item.description: arXiv:2610.15303v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) atomic-structure analysis is of central importance in (scanning) transmission electron microscopy (STEM). STEM techniques to reconstruct 3D structure include tilt-series or defocus-series annular dark-field, best suited to heavier atomic species, and dynamical-scattering-model inversion applied to single-defocus four-dimensional (4D) STEM data, requiring computationally expensive post-experiment analysis. In this study, we propose a 3D-structure linear inversion (3D LINV) STEM algorithm, which enables a fast and direct reconstruction of 3D structures from a single-defocus 4D-STEM dataset. This method is based on solving linear equations relating the measured 4D-STEM data and the unknown 3D specimen potential under the thick weak phase object approximation. We show the capabilities of 3D LINV STEM through systematic 4D-STEM simulations across various observation parameters such as specimen thickness, partial coherence, and shot noise, and through an experimental demonstration of 3D structure reconstruction of a stacked freestanding membrane with atomic-scale lateral resolution and nanometre-scale depth resolution.
item.dc:creator: Kousuke Ooe, Yufan Shen, Yuichi Shimakawa, Daisuke Kan, Scott D. Findlay

item.title: Local sensing of gas microflows using a levitated nanoparticle
item.description: arXiv:2610.15462v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Local measurements of gas flow in microscale geometries remain challenging due to the difficulty of micromechanical sensors implantation. Here, we use a levitated nanoparticle as a minimally invasive probe to map, with high spatial resolution, both the local pressure and velocity gas flow for a canonical example - a micropipe subjected to a pressure gradient. This technique enables characterization of nonequilibrium gas transport across several flow regimes, from slip flow to free-molecular flow. We directly observe the emergence of a nonlinear pressure distribution at large pressure ratios and obtain agreement with kinetic-theory predictions and Direct Simulation Monte Carlo calculations. These results introduce levitated nanoparticles as powerful and reconfigurable probes for microchannel gas sensing, with applications in microtechnology, micro-chemistry, and bioengineering.
item.dc:creator: Maxime Debiossac, David Grass, Daniel R. Ladiges, John E. Sader, Markus Aspelmeyer, Nikolai Kiesel

item.title: Non-Stationary Quantum Systems Associated with Stationary Scattering in One Dimension
item.description: arXiv:2610.15655v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Stationary scattering admits a dynamical formulation in which the scattering data are extracted from the evolution operator for an effective non-stationary and non-unitary quantum system. This provides a mathematical method of solving scattering problems. We consider the possibility of realizing such a quantum system and relating the scattering information to outcomes of quantum measurements performed on it. To this end, we examine stationary scattering problems in one dimension where the scattering data consist of reflection and transmission amplitudes and the corresponding effective quantum system is a non-unitary two-level system. The states of this system identify points in a Bloch sphere $S^2$ and their evolution yields trajectories in $S^2$. Quantum measurements turn out to be capable of providing information about the reflection amplitudes. We identify configurations displaying reflectionlessness with situations where one or both of the poles of $S^2$ undergo cyclic evolutions. Spectral singularities and coherent perfect absorption correspond to dynamical spin flips which map one of the poles of $S^2$ to the other.
item.dc:creator: Ali Mostafazadeh, Alireza Shariati Joni

item.title: Occultation polarimetry as a probe of unresolved polarization
item.description: arXiv:2610.15811v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Context: Low polarization in an unresolved source may reflect weak local polarization or spatial cancellation between strongly polarized regions. An occultation can break this spatial degeneracy by differentially sampling the source as the occulting boundary moves. Aims: We develop a general theoretical framework for occultation polarimetry and determine what information can be inferred directly from unresolved full Stokes light curves, without reconstructing a polarization image or prescribing a source model. Methods: For a stationary, spatially incoherent source undergoing monotonic occultation, we relate Stokes variations to the polarization sampled by an arbitrarily curved occulting boundary and derive an exact variance decomposition of the normalized Stokes vector. Results: The polarization deficit decomposes exactly into three non-negative contributions: local polarization deficit, mixing within limb samples, and mixing between their mean polarization states. The last is directly measurable and provides a sharp, model-independent lower bound on total spatial mixing. The associated covariance tensor further characterizes the direction and correlations of the resolved polarization variations, including those between linear and circular polarization. Finite sampling preserves the bound, which can be strengthened through complementary occultation trajectories. Conclusions: Occultation polarimetry provides a powerful observational technique for extracting quantitative, model independent constraints on spatial polarization mixing directly from unresolved Stokes light curves. It offers a means to reveal both the extent and the form of polarization structure otherwise inaccessible at the available angular resolution.
item.dc:creator: A. G. Tevzadze

item.title: Multipolar Nanophotonics with Quantum Computers
item.description: arXiv:2610.16062v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Small particles respond to light through electric and magnetic patterns called multipoles. Their interference determines the direction of scattered light and affects the decay of nearby emitters. Larger nanoantenna arrays, metasurfaces, and other nanophotonic systems demand increasingly costly simulations to meet strict performance and reliability requirements. We show how to represent these responses with quantum bits (qubits) and use quantum circuits to calculate scattering and the Purcell effect, the change in an emitter's decay rate caused by its surroundings. The circuits can encode known multipoles or estimate unknown ones from Maxwell's equations at the particle surface. We test the method against classical theory using an ideal quantum simulator and real IBM and IonQ quantum computers. For a silicon nanoparticle of radius 78 nm illuminated at 679 nm, IonQ gives a forward directivity of 2.984, close to the ideal dipolar value 3, quantifying the concentration of scattered light in the forward direction. For an emitter 10 nm from a gold nanoparticle and emitting at 510 nm, IBM measurements yield a calculated total decay rate 20.48 times its vacuum value versus 20.47 from theory, with correction for errors in reading the qubit states. We also establish how the number of multipoles and the required accuracy set the demands on qubits and measurements. These results motivate quantum-assisted design studies of directional radiation and emitter decay in nanophotonic systems.
item.dc:creator: Alex Krasnok

item.title: Metasurface quantum graphs for polarization-independent certified randomness
item.description: arXiv:2610.16286v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Quantum random number generators are crucial for information security, yet existing implementations are hindered by bulky optics, device imperfections, and state alignment constraints. Here, using a compact metasurface platform, we achieve polarization-independent certified randomness by establishing a quantitative quantum graph framework. By mapping multi-channel nanophotonic responses onto graph vertices, we assign metasurface measurements an operational information-theoretic meaning, directly connecting weighted graph degrees to conditional min-entropy estimation. The resulting graph-certified measurements yield robust private randomness even under entanglement-based attacks without complex optics. Experimentally, we fabricate 4- and 6-channel dielectric metasurfaces to implement high-dimensional positive operator-valued measure graphs, successfully certifying randomness with heralded single photons and Poissonian light. By integrating complex quantum measurements into a single passive layer, our metasurface quantum graphs provide a scalable route for integrated quantum technologies.
item.dc:creator: Xing Lin, Wenwen Liu, Wange Song, Sixin Chen, Shuang Zhang

item.title: Limit cycles govern wave energy accumulation in space-time-varying materials
item.description: arXiv:2610.16847v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the amplification and concentration of wave energy in smooth, periodic space-time media through the dynamics of the characteristic curves of the associated wave equation. In an impedance-matched setting, we show that stable limit cycles attract neighbouring characteristics, focusing the wave energy density. The exponential attraction rate is estimated analytically from the system's Lyapunov exponent. We further show that the attraction of characteristics and energy accumulation persist under a range of nonperiodic perturbations. Finally, we present a Floquet-Fourier numerical method for computing stable and unstable limit cycles and their attraction rates. Throughout, we exemplify the results using the example of modulation given by a superposition of travelling waves, revealing saddle--node bifurcations where limit cycles may appear depending on the relative wave speeds. Full-wave simulations confirm that the characteristic mechanism continues to describe energy accumulation beyond the impedance-matched case.
item.dc:creator: Bryn Davies, Erik Orvehed Hiltunen

item.title: Direct polarisation-state reconstruction with a temporal pointer: accessible states, resolution and optimal coupling
item.description: arXiv:2610.16871v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Weak measurements are used to amplify small signals, to address foundational questions, and to characterise quantum states without tomography. In direct state reconstruction each amplitude of the state vector is proportional to a single complex weak value, which for a temporal pointer is read from the mean arrival time and the mean frequency of the postselected pulse. Such an experiment requires three quantities to be fixed, the coupling, the angular resolution demanded of the reconstruction, and the set of states over which the method remains usable, and these are commonly set by the available apparatus rather than derived. We derive all three for a Gaussian temporal pointer and an arbitrary postselection state. The states that cannot be reconstructed form a spherical cap centred on the state orthogonal to the postselection, whose geodesic half-angle follows from the largest of three independent thresholds and involves no adjustable parameter. Two states are distinguishable only if they differ by more than a minimal step fixed by the coupling, by the number of incident photons and by the sensitivity of the weak value along the path followed. For an inversion at first order in the coupling the systematic and statistical errors are opposed and fix an optimal coupling that varies as the inverse sixth root of the number of incident photons, whereas an exact inversion at finite coupling removes the systematic error, the remaining bound being one on the two-centroid readout rather than on the inversion, since below an amplitude equal to a quarter of the coupling two states give the same pair of centroids while their profiles differ. These results allow a direct reconstruction experiment to be dimensioned before the apparatus is assembled.
item.dc:creator: Shane P. Gervais, Lambert Giner

item.title: Spatial Engineering of Topological Quantum Matter with Structured Light
item.description: arXiv:2610.17181v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Structured light provides a powerful means of controlling matter while itself exhibiting nontrivial spatial topology. Here, we show that these spatial structures can be harnessed to locally engineer the topological properties of matter. In a paradigmatic example of a topological insulator with Dirac surface states driven by an optical skyrmion beam, we show that structured light spatially tailors the effective Hamiltonian, yielding position-dependent topological gaps and Dirac velocities. The resulting gap modulation can create topological and trivial regions separated by optically defined interfaces, without introducing material boundaries or chemical modifications. We further show that the geometry of these interfaces can be controlled through the spatial structure of the light, in particular its orbital angular momentum. Our results establish structured light as a route to dynamically pattern topological phases and open a broader perspective on the interplay between topology in light and matter, including the possibility of transferring topological characteristics between the two.
item.dc:creator: Matias Mustonen, Ali G. Moghaddam, Teemu Ojanen, Marco Ornigotti

item.title: Ghost unitaries for loss-resilient photonic resource-state generation
item.description: arXiv:2610.17300v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Entangled few-photon states, such as Bell and Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) states, are central resources for discrete-variable photonic quantum information processing. In many architectures, these states are generated probabilistically by first heralding single photons from biphoton sources and then interfering them in linear-optical circuits. In this work, we show that the entanglement structure of said biphoton sources can be directly exploited for noise-engineering to deliver higher quality resource states. Using the transpose identity of multi-mode squeezed vacuum states, we introduce "ghost-unitary" implementations in which the target resource-generation interferometer is applied to the heralding modes rather than to the delivered resource modes. When the dominant imperfection is interferometric loss, this relocation converts direct amplitude damping of the output into false-positive heralding events that require both higher-pair emission and photon loss. In the low-squeezing regime, these events are parametrically suppressed, yielding higher-fidelity conditional resource states. We analyze this mechanism for single-qubit states, two-photon NOON states, Bell states, and a family of $n$-qubit GHZ states, as well as for single-qubit teleportation and type-I-fusion-based resource growth. Across these examples, we delineate finite parameter regimes in which ghost-unitary implementations outperform direct implementations, with particular relevance to frequency-bin photonics where active linear-optical transformations can be relatively lossy. We also prove that, in the setting considered here, the direct implementation of the $n$-GHZ family delivers identically damped outputs: equivalent to the ideal state followed by uniform amplitude damping. This extends the known $n=2,3$ cases and provides a structural result of independent interest for photonic quantum information processing.
item.dc:creator: Kevin J. Randles, Manuel H. Mu\~noz-Arias, Kevin Thompson

item.title: A complete forward projection algorithm through cylindrical and spherical refractive windows
item.description: arXiv:2610.17413v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Cylindrical or spherical windows often appear in experiments and real applications. Measuring through those windows requires projecting 3D points to pixels, which is different to compute due to refraction. A point may have multiple projected images but cannot be efficiently determine with the existing projection algorithms. Using the ray's conserved momenta, we reduce this projection to closed-form equations with a concave structure. As a result, we can successfully determine whether a 3D point has a single projection or multiple and compute those locations. In simulations, with one single search, we can recover images that iterative methods miss even with many restarts. A wand calibration based on it can reach the precision limit set by image noise, enabling accurate 3D particle tracking in a swirling flow through cylinder windows. This algorithm shows how to predict visibility and multiple images through curved windows, shedding light for 3D pipe flow measurements, accurate underwater reconstruction, and many real applications.
item.dc:creator: Shijie Zhong, Shiyong Tan, Xiaosi Zhang, Yanying Li, Rui Ni

item.title: Mathematical framework for simulation of non-perturbative cavity optomechanics with plate-like dielectrics
item.description: arXiv:2610.17475v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Cavity optomechanical models typically treat a sensor either as a perturbative polarizable object in a pre-existing optical field, or solve the field at a fixed equilibrium and linearize in a fixed optical-mode basis. Neither self-consistently determines the spatially resolved cavity field, the optical force, the mechanical equilibrium, and the back-action when a finite-thickness dielectric plate intercepts the entire optical mode and restructures the intracavity field. In this companion paper to [1], we develop that treatment by extending the vacuum two-photon formalism to finite-thickness planar dielectrics, incorporating their Fresnel reflection, internal propagation, optical forces, and mechanical back-action directly into the field equations. We derive the carrier and sideband transfer functions needed to describe the coupled optical-mechanical system, including optomechanical cooling and the response to external perturbations. The result is a systematic starting point for calculating detector response and noise budgets for cavity experiments with intracavity dielectrics, including gravitational wave detectors deploying levitated sensors.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Laeuger, Nancy Aggarwal

item.title: Background2Background: a self-supervised background removal framework for high dimensional microscopy
item.description: arXiv:2610.17615v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: High-dimensional microscopy captures features across space, time, and spectrum, but complex backgrounds obscure signals. We present Background2Background (B2B), a self-supervised background removal framework leveraging the backgrounds larger correlation relative to the signal. Local pixel shuffling disrupts signal correlations while preserving background structure, transforming signals into effective noise for Noise2Noise-based background removal. Across fluorescence, stimulated Raman scattering and mid-infrared photothermal imaging, B2B achieves over 40-fold background suppression and reveals hidden signatures.
item.dc:creator: Guangrui Ding, Haonan Lin, Rong Tang, Bethany Weinberg, Jianpeng Ao, Qing Xia, Guorong Hu, Dingcheng Sun, Jiaze Yin, Lei Tian, Ji-Xin Cheng

item.title: Boson Sampling Using Fock States from On-Demand Single Photon Source Arrays: Quantum Complexity & Impact of Dephasing
item.description: arXiv:2610.17773v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Boson sampling with array of on-demand single photons (discreet variable Fock states) as resource states provides distinct advantages in complexity scaling compared to single photon resource states mimicked by the states (continuous variable) generated in nonlinear photonics. Recent progress in realization of regular ordered array of mesa top single quantum dots (MTSQDs) enabling on-demand generation of many photon resource states with high single photon purity and indistinguishability [1,2] has opened the possibility of implementing chip-scale Boson sampling with single photons. An important question towards scale up of such circuits is how the dephasing and decay timescale of individual on-demand single photons affect the final probability distribution of the N-photon entangled state. In this work we report a framework that provides direct link between the physical sources of decoherence to the outcome of multiphoton correlation measurements. We explicitly incorporate the symmetrization of the N-photon states while accounting for the shape of the individual wave packets and dephasing. Using this framework, we show predictive estimates of the probability of generation of a 4-photon NOON state using an optical circuit initialized with 4 identical single photon wave packets, mimicking the emitted photons from MTSQD single photon sources reported in [2]. Specifically, we show how the probability of generating various 4-photon entangled states depend on the two-photon interference visibility which is determined by the pure dephasing timescale in relation to the radiative decay timescale. The results provide quantitative guidelines to measure 4 photon and higher number of entangled photon states generated in an optical circuit with on demand single photon sources and provide a link between physical processes such as temperature and the output state of the quantum optical circuits.
item.dc:creator: Swarnabha Chattaraj, Anupam Madhukar

item.title: Theory of Sub-Doppler Spectroscopy of Alkali Metal Vapors in the Field of Counterpropagating Bichromatic Laser Beams: Probe Beam Regime
item.description: arXiv:2610.18372v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Sub-Doppler resonances observed in miniature cells ($V \ll 1 cm^3$) with Rb or Cs atoms in the field of counterpropagating bichromatic laser beams are of interest for the creation of a miniature quantum frequency standard (QFS) of the optical range. However, a theory of these resonances that takes into full account the real structure of energy levels in an atom has not yet been constructed, which would make it possible to obtain explicit analytical expressions for the absorption coefficient of the medium. This paper addresses this gap using the density matrix formalism and the algebra of irreducible tensor operators. Namely, we obtained an analytical expression for the absorption coefficient of the probe beam in the presence of a more intense counterpropagating beam (pump-probe regime). Moreover, the calculations were carried out for arbitrary parameters of laser beam polarization, arbitrary angular momenta of optical dipole transitions in the atom and various relaxation processes. The constructed theory allows us to correctly take into account the simultaneous action of various nonlinear optical effects, in contrast to the simplified three-level model of the atom, and also to investigate the partial contribution of each of them to the overall observed resonant circuit. The analysis performed, in particular, made it possible to predict an increase in the amplitude of the sub-Doppler resonance when using counterpropagating light beams with opposite circular polarizations in relation to the configuration of counterpropagating beams with orthogonal linear polarizations, which is often used in practice.
item.dc:creator: A. M. Mikhailov, D. V. Brazhnikov

item.title: Spectral Theory of an Exactly Solvable Quantum-Optical Oscillator
item.dc:creator: Sam Johar, Joseph Kraisler

item.title: Generalized Time-Reversal for Pulse Control in Diffusive Media
item.description: arXiv:2509.10646v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Time-reversal symmetry allows waves to retrace their paths through complex media and refocus at their origin. However, incomplete capture and reversal of scattered waves often limit pulse recovery. We address this challenge for spatially extended sources by introducing a generalized time-reversal framework, which identifies the optimal source pattern as the one that maximizes the energy of the waves that are captured and reversed. We experimentally verify it in a two-dimensional diffusive waveguide, showing the peak transmitted power at the recovery time is doubled over standard time-reversal. Internal spatiotemporal dynamics, reconstructed from frequency-resolved measurements, reveal a ``loading and firing" process in which energy accumulates within the medium and then is released abruptly. Time-reversing this burst enables deep energy delivery into the scattering medium. Generalized time-reversal opens new possibilities for short-pulse control in scattering media, with applications ranging from optogenetics to random laser amplification.
item.dc:creator: Rohin E. McIntosh, Arthur Goetschy, Alexey Yamilov, Nicholas Bender, Hasan Yilmaz, Hui Cao

item.title: Inverse-Designed Superchiral Hot Spot in Dielectric Meta-Cavity Toward Ultra-Compact Enantioselective Detection
item.description: arXiv:2512.19917v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Chiral nanophotonic structures have garnered considerable interest in recent years due to their potential to enhance the efficacy of chirality-sensitive biomolecular detection. Designing metaplatforms to enhance chiroptical signals under linearly polarized excitation is particularly appealing due to the minimal chiral background and the ease of controlling excitation polarization. Here, a novel two-step inverse design scheme for dielectric lossless metasurfaces with superchiral hot spots is proposed. The method extends the local density of field enhancements for non-chiral fields into the chiral regime and significantly surpasses previous enhancements in superchiral field generation. It has been demonstrated that by leveraging the excitation of high quality factor modes with small mode volumes, it is theoretically possible to convert linearly polarized plane waves into a superchiral hot spot with record-high enhancement in the near-field optical chirality up to 10^4. A prototype is successfully implemented using advanced nanofabrication technologies. The optical characterization of the prototype demonstrates a 10^2-fold enhancement in optical chirality. The findings of this study unveil novel prospects for chiral spectroscopy with ultra-compact devices, underscoring the role of machine learning and physics-based inverse design in the development of cutting-edge, functional photonic structures.

item.title: Cathodoluminescence Wavefront Retrieval
item.description: arXiv:2605.21944v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Free-electron-based nanoscopy enables the study of optical excitations in materials with deep-subwavelength spatial resolution, with cathodoluminescence (CL) being one of the most useful resulting signals. When combined with an optical collection system, CL measurements can access multidimensional information of light; yet the phase of the emitted optical fields has remained largely elusive. Here, we demonstrate a reference-free phase retrieval approach for far-field CL wavefronts using the Gerchberg-Saxton algorithm implemented with real-space and angular-space CL intensity data. Applying this approach to representative nanostructures, including a planar surface, nanosphere, plasmonic crystal, and nanowire, we reconstruct distinct phase distributions that reveal their underlying radiation mechanisms. This reference-free framework offers a robust and flexible route for retrieving the phase of electron-beam-excited optical fields without relying on a reference wave, making it readily extendable to a wide range of nanostructures.
item.dc:creator: Izzah Machfuudzoh, Ryoichi Horisaki, Takumi Sannomiya

item.title: Nanoscopic Multiplexing Optical Data Storage via Chip Fabrication
item.description: arXiv:2605.29999v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The accelerating growth of global data demands storage technologies combining high capacity, long lifetime and low energy consumption. Optical storage is attractive for archival applications, but conventional optical writing is constrained by diffraction-limited resolution and scalability, while thermal accumulation limits high-speed writing. Here we shift optical data writing from a serial optical process to a fabrication-defined process, in which lithographic masks govern where material modification occurs. Using patterned resist masks and ion implantation, we create fluorescent information voxels with nanoscale control over millimeter-scale areas. The platform supports multilevel and multidimensional encoding by independently encoding information in fluorescence intensity and wavelength. A machine-learning-assisted super-resolution reconstruction protocol is developed to recover information beyond conventional optical resolution for information readout. Overall, the framework reaches an areal storage capacity of 1.1 Tbit within the area of a standard 120-mm optical disc, approximately fivefold that of a conventional single-layer Blu-ray disc. This architecture establishes a micro/nanofabrication-compatible route to scalable optical memory and opens a pathway to wafer-scale archival storage.
item.dc:creator: Junyu Guan, Quanshen Shen, Bowen Tong, Hanzhi Wang, Zeyu Gao, Hanyu Zhang, Jingyang Zhou, Zihua Chai, Dong Liu, Ya Wang, Kangwei Xia

item.title: Multi-pulse accumulation of gas molecular coherence enables gigahertz ultrafast frequency conversion
item.description: arXiv:2606.11811v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Frequency conversion of ultrafast lasers is fundamentally constrained by the trade-off between pulse energy and repetition rate. Here, we demonstrate a frequency conversion mechanism in which molecular coherence accumulates across ultrafast pulse trains in gas-filled hollow-core fibers. Unlike conventional nonlinear interactions initiated by individual high-energy pulses, this mechanism relies on the collective buildup of coherent molecular oscillations driven by successive pulses. Using this approach, we achieve Raman frequency conversion at repetition rates up to 3 GHz with nanojoule pulse energies. The results demonstrate that accumulated molecular coherence can govern nonlinear frequency conversion, revealing a domain of light-matter interaction whose physical limits remain largely unexplored.

item.title: Generation of continuous-wave laser light at 148.4 nm using cavity-enhanced second harmonic generation in $BaMgF_4$
item.description: arXiv:2606.25046v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The development of a nuclear optical clock based on \textsuperscript{229}Th is expected to influence the next generation of time and frequency standards. At its heart is the need for a continuous wave (CW) at laser at 148.4~nm to drive the clock transition between the ground and excited isomeric state. In this work we experimentally investigate the potential of BaMgF\textsubscript{4} crystals to create a CW solid state laser at the vacuum ultraviolet (VUV) wavelength of 148.4~nm via cavity-enhanced second harmonic generation. For this purpose, a BaMgF\textsubscript{4} crystal was grown, optically polished and periodically poled. The crystal was inserted into a power-enhancement cavity, resonant at the fundamental wavelength of 296.8~nm and the generated laser light at 148.4~nm was characterized. Within this proof-of-concept investigation, a VUV output power of typically ($16\pm1$)~pW is obtained. This marks the first time that this type of crystal is used to generate VUV laser light. The experimental findings are compared to theoretical expectations and provide a clear path for future improvements, which could have implications not only for compact laser sources in the VUV but also solid-state as well as single-ion based \textsuperscript{229}Th nuclear clocks.

item.title: Optical Amplification with Large Goos-H$\ddot{a}$nchen Shift Driven by Non-Hermitian Bilayer Meta-Grating Under Lasing State
item.description: arXiv:2606.31060v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The coexistence of gain and loss in parity-time symmetric bilayer meta-gratings enables the transformation of bound states in the continuum into a ring of lasing threshold modes. Under lasing state, gain saturation drives the contraction of this mode ring into a single discrete lasing point. Additionally incident weak optical field with frequency and incident angle nearly matched to the lasing mode can obtain amplification accompanied by prominent Goos-H$\ddot{a}$nchen shifts. Specifically, active meta-grating with lasing mode at the $\Gamma$ point induce sizable Goos-H$\ddot{a}$nchen shifts. In contrast, active meta-grating with lasing mode off the $\Gamma$ point induce large Goos-H$\ddot{a}$nchen shifts that are proportional to the quality factor of the effective resonant modes under lasing state. In finite meta-grating, finite-size effects exert distinct influences on the lasing state as well as the Goos-H$\ddot{a}$nchen shifts of the additionally incident optical field: the lasing characteristics and Goos-H$\ddot{a}$nchen shifts of $\Gamma$-point lasing modes remain nearly unaffected, whereas those of off-$\Gamma$ lasing modes are significantly modulated by finite-size perturbations.
item.dc:creator: Ma Luo, Xueyi Zhang

item.title: Optomechanical transducers for gigahertz frequency ultrasound imaging
item.description: arXiv:2607.02936v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Ultrasound is a noninvasive, real-time, and therefore widely used imaging modality; yet its application in cellular and sub-cellular biology is significantly limited by rapidly increasing acoustic losses in aqueous solutions with decreasing wavelength. Here we introduce a nano-optomechanical cavity transducer platform to generate and detect ultrasound in aqueous solutions with a sub-micron acoustic wavelength. We analyze the full signal pathway through a combination of finite element method modeling and the coupled differential equations that describe the dispersive optomechanical interaction. Our findings project a signal-to-noise ratio in the thousands at ~5 GHz, limited by diffraction losses and thermal-acoustic noise. This work establishes a viable path towards optomechanical ultrasound systems capable of label-free imaging at cellular and sub-cellular length scales while also providing a broader framework for optomechanical crystal device operation in aqueous environments relevant to biochemical sensing, medical diagnostics, underwater acoustic sensing, and nanoscale imaging.
item.dc:creator: Lisa Hackett, Chang Ge, Alex Miera, Brandon Smith, Matt Eichenfield

item.title: Flexible Inverse Design of Optical Multilayer Coatings Using Discrete-Continuous Flow Matching
item.description: arXiv:2607.08392v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Optical multilayer coatings are used in imaging optics, lasers, telecommunications, solar cells, and radiative cooling, where the spectral response required by each application is achieved by a well-designed layer structure. However, existing design methods have limitations. Local methods refine a starting design efficiently but depend on its quality, and global searches require up to millions of transfer-matrix evaluations per target. Existing deep-learning inverse-design models are fast, but they are trained for a fixed set of materials and a fixed wavelength band, and they either optimize the thicknesses for a fixed material sequence or choose them from a discrete grid. In this paper, we present IrisFlow, a generative model that addresses these limitations by taking each candidate material as its optical constants and the target spectrum together with its wavelengths as input. It generates the material and the continuous thickness of every layer jointly, by coupled discrete and continuous flow matching in a single network. We demonstrate its performance through design with materials outside the training library and on bands beyond the training range, and through comparisons with classical optimizers and an existing deep-learning model. We also demonstrate its usability in a practical design workflow by designing four colored solar-reflective coatings with the calibrated optical constants of an existing deposition system. Combined with a local refinement of its ten best designs, it reduces the number of transfer-matrix evaluations about 500-fold relative to needle optimization at comparable accuracy. The code, trained model, and training and test data are publicly available.
item.dc:creator: Zhiyi Li, Yuheng Jin, Yidan Huang, Nan Chen, Hongyan Fu, Yikun Bu

item.title: Photonic reservoir computing with complex networks
item.description: arXiv:2607.23285v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Photonic reservoir computing has attracted increasing attention as a fast and low-cost approach for time-series prediction. Photonic reservoir computing utilizes the high speed, broad bandwidth, and spatial parallelism of light. However, the effect of the internal connection structure (network topology) on the computing performance has not been investigated for large-scale photonic reservoirs. In this study, we experimentally and numerically demonstrate photonic reservoir computing using a spatial light modulator to systematically evaluate the relationship between the network topology and the performance of reservoir computing. We introduce complex network structures such as small-world and scale-free network topologies of the internal nodes in the reservoir. We perform the memory capacity measurement and the one-step-ahead prediction task of the chaotic time series to compare the performance. We found that the small-world network exhibits the maximum memory capacity and the best prediction performance. Our numerical calculations reveal that the performance of the time-series prediction can be optimized by changing the rewiring probability of the network and the leak rate of the reservoir. We also implement photonic human brain network as a reservoir, which is designed by the connectomes of human brain activities. We found that the network topology strongly affects the performance of reservoir computing, and the small-world network structure outperforms the other configurations.

item.title: Approximate reservoir computing with a semiconductor laser for reducing energy consumption
item.description: arXiv:2607.23288v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Photonic reservoir computing is a promising physical machine-learning approach for time-series prediction. Quantization of the reservoir response signal is an important consideration in the implementation of photonic reservoir computing, and the number of quantization bits and sampling frequency need to be optimized to achieve high prediction performance and low energy consumption. However, few studies have investigated the effects of the number of quantization bits and sampling frequency on both prediction performance and energy consumption. In this study, we introduce the concept of approximate reservoir computing with a semiconductor laser by quantizing the reservoir node states and output weights. We numerically evaluate the performance of a chaotic time-series prediction task and estimate the energy consumption per sample using a component-level model. By optimizing the number of quantization bits, the sampling frequency, and the injection current of the semiconductor laser, we achieve a significant reduction in the estimated energy consumption per sample while maintaining prediction performance. We also obtain model-based estimates of the throughput, energy efficiency, and energy per operation of the proposed reservoir-computing system.
item.dc:creator: Tatsuki Ito, Kazutaka Kanno, Satoshi Kawakami, Atsushi Uchida

item.title: The vanishing distance: a depth-range boundary for dynamic wavefront shaping
item.description: arXiv:2608.17551v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Optical imaging and transmission through scattering media conventionally rely on ballistic light, whose power decays exponentially with the optical thickness. Although ballistic light cannot be exploited beyond a certain depth, no simple criterion currently identifies this limit. Therefore, we introduce here the vanishing distance that is defined as the propagation length at which the ballistic power equals the power carried by a single diffuse optical mode. Beyond the vanishing distance, multiply scattered light dominates, which can be harnessed by optical wavefront shaping or by computational reconstructions. We present a simple semi-analytical model for radiance propagation, validated by Monte Carlo simulations and by experiments in both monodisperse and heterogeneous scattering media. From these data, we estimate the vanishing distance and the associated minimum source power. Across representative scattering environments, ballistic light vanishes after about 20 to 40 scattering mean free paths. Unlike the transport mean free path that characterizes the angular randomization of the scattered light, the vanishing distance identifies the loss of the ballistic channel on a modal-power basis. The vanishing distance is thus a two-sided bound: ballistic approaches cannot be efficiently applied beyond it, whereas wavefront shaping of scattered light offers no advantage below it.

item.title: Dual-Symmetrized Construction of Electromagnetic Beams Beyond the Paraxial Approximation with an Explicit Separation of Scalar and Vectorial Corrections
item.description: arXiv:2608.26776v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop a perturbative framework for constructing the fields of electromagnetic beams beyond the paraxial approximation, in which the vectorial correction is shared symmetrically between the electric and magnetic fields and separated from the isotropic scalar correction. The method is based on a direct iterative derivation from Maxwell equations and combines complementary electric-first and magnetic-first constructions, thereby removing the construction-dependent assignment of the vectorial correction to either the electric or magnetic field. In addition, the scalar envelope correction is obtained independently from the isotropic co-polar contribution to the solutions of the higher-order Helmholtz equation. The resulting corrected fields apply to an arbitrary paraxial envelope and input Jones polarization.

item.title: Nonlinear Photoemission for Bright Beams in X-Band Photoinjectors
item.description: arXiv:2609.04571v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The ongoing development of low-cost and compact x-ray light sources is vital for increasing the number of experiments that can be performed at the atomic scale. One option for a compact and simple photoinjector is to operate in blow-out mode, in which a high-charge, short-bunch length electron beam self-expands by space-charge forces into a uniformly ellipsoidal shape. This mode necessitates a photoinjector whose initial electron pulse has a pulse duration on the order of $100$ fs. A photoinjector utilizing linear photoemission with an ultraviolet laser in this regime presents significant technical challenges, as many optical substrates degrade at these wavelengths. In this paper, we present an alternative design that uses nonlinear photoemission to produce electron beams with high charge and short bunch length in an X-band (9300 MHz) photoinjector. This photoinjector design produces an electron beam with a bunch charge of up to $200$ pC, an RMS bunch length of $291$ fs, a normalized transverse emittance of $1$ to $1.4$ mm$\cdot$mrad, and an energy spread of $10^{-4}$. This results in a beam brightness of $10^{18}$ A/m$^2$, which is bright enough for our beamline's purposes. We also present ongoing efforts are aimed at further increasing the electron beam brightness by using a spatial light modulator to shape the laser profile at the cathode.

item.title: Fabrication-Aware Design of a Hybrid Metasurface-Bragg Mirror for Low-Noise Precision Optics
item.description: arXiv:2609.05001v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: High-reflectivity coatings for precision interferometry must simultaneously minimize optical losses and thermally driven displacement noise. Dielectric Bragg mirrors provide robust high reflectance but rely on thick multilayer coatings, whereas metasurface mirrors provide high reflectance and low noise but are sensitive to fabrication-induced deviations. A fabrication-aware photonic design framework is introduced that combines a resonant single-layer metasurface, an etch-stop layer, an antiresonant spacer, and a reduced Bragg reflector. Fabrication effects, including geometric tolerances and line-edge roughness, are explicitly considered in the optical design. Full-wave electromagnetic simulations are combined with a truncated-Gaussian Monte Carlo analysis to determine the performance distribution under the assumed fabrication conditions. The ideal metasurface design achieves a modeled non-reflected power of $1-R<10^{-5}$. After roughness-aware reoptimization, the modeled non-reflected power remains below $1.04\cdot10^{-4}$ at $80\%$ fabrication yield. For the cryogenic ETpathfinder gravitational-wave testbed, two Bragg layer pairs reduce the non-reflected power of the complete stack to approximately $6.6\,\mathrm{ppm}$. The estimated thermal displacement-noise amplitude spectral density is $1.97\cdot10^{-20}\,\mathrm{m/\sqrt{Hz}}$ at $100\,\mathrm{Hz}$. The architecture connects fabrication robustness, optical performance, and thermal-noise reduction within a single design framework.
item.dc:creator: Mika Gaedtke, Christian Kranhold, Markus Walther, Falk Eilenberger, Stefanie Kroker, Thomas Siefke

item.title: Tunable hyperbolic metamaterials for brightening single-photon emission
item.description: arXiv:2609.30179v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Hyperbolic metamaterials (HMMs) are widely used to enhance spontaneous emission through their exceptionally large photonic density of states, yet large Purcell factors (>100) rarely translate into brighter emission, exposing both a practical limitation of HMMs as brightening platforms and a flaw in the Purcell factor itself as a figure of merit. Here we systematically evaluate spontaneous emission enhancement and photon outcoupling in metal-dielectric HMMs (TiO$_2$/Ag and phase-change Sb$_2$S$_3$/Ag) using effective medium theory, transfer matrix calculations, and full-wave FDTD simulations. We show that planar HMMs with Purcell factors exceeding 100 have external quantum efficiencies below 0.01, yielding an actual radiative Purcell factor (PF$_{rad}$) of only 1-2. Nanopatterning the HMM into a photonic crystal efficiently couples trapped high-k modes into free space, raising PF$_{rad}$ by an order of magnitude. Incorporating the phase-change material Sb$_2$S$_3$ further enables dynamic tuning of the hyperbolic spectral window and active control over emission brightness: an optimized nanostructured design reaches PF$_{rad}$ ~ 10-15 in the near-infrared, with switching contrast exceeding a factor of 15 upon phase transition. These results establish the radiative Purcell factor as a more reliable figure of merit than the conventional Purcell factor for engineering quantum emitters, and provide a practical route toward actively tunable, bright single-photon sources based on hyperbolic metamaterials.

item.title: Nonreciprocal Polychromatic Radiation from a Space-Time-Modulated Omega-Topology Meta-Transceiver
item.description: arXiv:2609.38542v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Time-modulated metasurfaces offer a magnet-free route to nonreciprocal wave control, but existing realizations modulate only the electric response of the structure, and proposals for simultaneous electric-magnetic modulation have so far remained theoretical. We experimentally demonstrate a space-time-periodic meta-transceiver whose omega-topology unit cell integrates varactor-loaded electric (dipole) and magnetic (ring) resonators, both modulated by a common unidirectional traveling-wave bias. This modulation gives rise to two independent, experimentally resolved manifestations of nonreciprocity: on transmit, the incident field is efficiently converted into a polychromatic comb of harmonics that radiate at distinct, bias-reconfigurable angles, while on receive, the same modulation instead suppresses frequency conversion and routes the incoming wave preferentially toward one port over the other. These two effects - nonreciprocal polychromatic conversion and unidirectional wave routing - arise from a single unidirectional space-time modulation but act on distinct physical observables, frequency content and spatial direction, respectively. Measured near the electric resonance with a shared bias, these effects characterize the complete cell and do not separate its electric and magnetic contributions. Our results establish the space-time-modulated omega-topology cell as an experimentally viable platform for reconfigurable, full-duplex nonreciprocal wave transformation.
item.dc:creator: Sajjad Taravati, Ya-Adama Kabia

item.title: Angular resolution limit of augmented reality waveguides from guided mode theory
item.description: arXiv:2610.09527v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We derive the angular resolution limit of an augmented-reality (AR) waveguide combiner from guided mode theory. A slab of finite thickness supports only a discrete set of total-internal-reflection (TIR) angles, giving an angular resolution that worsens with thinner waveguides and smaller TIR angles. At 500~$\mu$m thickness the resolution is worse than the 1 arcmin (60 ppd) acuity target over most of the usable TIR range, and reaching 1 arcmin for TIR < 42$^\circ$ requires a substrate thicker than 1 mm. The limit is washed out by a source linewidth above $\sim$0.1~nm or a thickness variation above $\sim$100~nm across the pupil-replication period, but only partially by pupil truncation and not at all by out-coupling loss. LED- and micro-LED-based displays are therefore unaffected, owing to their broad spectra, whereas a narrow-linewidth laser-based display in a thin, uniform waveguide is subject to this limit.
item.dc:creator: Guohua Wei

item.title: Inverse Design of Integrated Photonic Components for Visible-Light Applications
item.description: arXiv:2610.11453v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Photonic integrated circuits (PICs) operating in the visible spectral range are crucial for quantum technologies, optical sensing, and nonlinear optics applications. However, their development is hampered by limited integration density and operational bandwidth, linked to low refractive index contrast and restricted parameter space in intuition-based PIC design. We address these bottlenecks with an adjoint-based, fabrication-aware inverse design workflow tailored for visible-spectrum photonics. By expanding the capabilities of FDTDX, an open-source, GPU-accelerated FDTD solver, we provide a versatile memory and runtime efficient inverse design platform. Demonstrating this approach on a silicon nitride (Si3N4) platform, we design, fabricate, and experimentally validate ultra-compact, broadband components for light routing, multiplexing, and polarization control. This work provides a scalable framework for high-density, high-performance visible-light PICs.
item.dc:creator: Christoph Stockinger, Marko \v{S}imi\'c, John O. Adeniran, Natale G. Pruiti, Marc Sorel, Peter Banzer

item.title: Harnessing Machine Learning for Ultrafast Science in Facility Settings: Opportunities and Challenges
item.description: arXiv:2610.12146v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Ultrafast science is rapidly evolving from a collection of specialized laser experiments into a facility-scale, data-intensive research endeavour. High-repetition-rate femtosecond and attosecond sources, synchronized multidimensional diagnostics, and increasingly nonlinear laser-matter interactions now generate heterogeneous data streams whose volume, speed, and complexity often exceed the capacity of conventional manual workflows. This chapter examines how machine learning can become an enabling layer for next-generation ultrafast facilities, with emphasis on the Extreme Light Infrastructure (ELI) ecosystem. We discuss the scientific drivers for artificial-intelligence-assisted experimentation, propose a facility-scale digital architecture spanning acquisition, ingestion, storage, analytics, machine learning, adaptive feedback, and user interfaces, and review representative examples from ELI ALPS, ELI Beamlines, and ELI-NP. The central thesis is that machine learning should not be treated merely as an offline data-analysis tool; rather, when constrained by physical insight and embedded in robust data infrastructure, it can support real-time diagnostics, surrogate modeling, anomaly detection, experimental optimization, and progressively autonomous discovery workflows.
item.dc:creator: Mousumi Upadhyay Kahaly, Ishraq Md Anjum, Davorin Peceli, Zsolt Divek, Subhendu Kahaly

item.title: Photon pairs, squeezed light and the quantum wave mixing effect in a cascaded qubit system
item.description: arXiv:2604.08139v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We develop a theoretical description of quantum wave mixing (QWM) in a cascaded waveguide-QED system of two superconducting qubits, where the probe is driven by an external coherent tone and by the resonance fluorescence of a strongly driven source qubit. Starting from the field correlation functions of the source emission, we derive an effective master-equation treatment for the probe and identify the regime in which the incident fluorescence is characterized by anomalous correlations. When the coherent Rayleigh component of the source spectrum is suppressed, the probe equations of motion become equivalent to those for a qubit driven by a coherent tone and broadband squeezed light, although the ligt emitted by the source is non-Gaussian and antibunched. This equivalence implies a selection rule for the peaks of the QWM spectrum, with a strong suppression of sidebands associated with processes involving an odd number of photons taken from the source field. Numerical simulations of the full cascaded two-qubit model for different ratios of radiative decay rates unambiguously confirm the participation of correlated photon pairs in QWM processes. The current research illustrates that the analysis of peak amplitudes can be used to probe photon statistics in the incident nonclassical field.
item.dc:creator: R. D. Ivanovskikh, W. V. Pogosov, A. A. Elistratov, S. V. Remizov, A. Yu. Dmitriev, T. R. Sabirov, A. V. Vasenin, S. A. Gunin, O. V. Astafiev

item.title: Pressure-induced decoupling of the pseudogap and superconductivity in a bilayer cuprate
item.description: arXiv:2604.10207v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The physical origin of the pseudogap in cuprate superconductors, whether a precursor to superconductivity or a distinct intertwined order, remains an open question. Although hydrostatic pressure provides a clean tuning parameter, probing the relevant energy scales under compression has remained experimentally elusive. Here, we employ ultrafast optical spectroscopy to track the non-equilibrium quasiparticle dynamics of slightly underdoped Bi$_2$Sr$_2$CaCu$_2$O$_{8+{\delta}}$ up to 37 GPa. By disentangling the pseudogap and superconducting relaxation channels in the time domain, we uncover a contrasting pressure evolution: despite an increase in carrier density, the pseudogap thermal onset (T$^*$) rises monotonically, whereas its energy gap ($\Delta_{PG}$) is continuously suppressed. Conversely, the critical temperature (T$_C$) and the superconducting gap ($\Delta_{SC}$) exhibit a synchronized dome-like trajectory. The effective coupling ratio 2$\Delta_{SC}$/k$_B$T$_C$ collapses abruptly from ~10 toward the weak-coupling d-wave limit, signifying a crossover from a phase-fluctuating two-dimensional regime to a globally coherent three-dimensional state. Upon compression to 37 GPa, the superconducting condensate is completely quenched into an insulating-like state, yet the pseudogap persists. The extended phase diagram reveals an unambiguous decoupling between the pseudogap and superconductivity, imposing stringent constraints on microscopic theories of high-temperature superconductivity.
item.dc:creator: Yanghao Meng, Wenjin Mao, Liucheng Chen, Elbert E. M. Chia, Yifeng Yang, Tao Xiang, Jianlin Luo, Lin Zhao, Xingjiang Zhou, Xiaohui Yu, Xinbo Wang

item.title: Entanglement and photoelectron holography in dissociative photoionization: molecular quantum eraser
item.description: arXiv:2604.16107v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In a double-slit experiment with a bipartite system, the visibility of interference fringes depends on the availability of which-way information. Here, we report a Bell-like state of photoelectron and residual ion in the multiphoton dissociative ionization of the D$_2$ molecule. Evidence for entanglement is provided by the correlated emission directions of photoelectron and ion, which is observed using a COLTRIMS reaction microscope. In the presence of this correlation, the holographic interference fringes contained in the photoelectron momentum distributions are suppressed, indicating the existence of which-way information. The interference pattern persists when a single ionic state is populated and thus no which-way information is available. The experimental observations and conclusions are supported by the numerical solution of the electronic-nuclear time-dependent Schr\"odinger equation. Our work demonstrates that coincidence spectroscopy of ions and electrons is a powerful method for studying fundamental concepts of quantum information science within the context of ultrafast light-matter interactions.

item.title: Breakdown of Fluctuational Electrodynamics in the Extreme Near Field
item.description: arXiv:2606.05845v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Fluctuational electrodynamics relies on the assumption that thermal fluctuations in distinct bodies are statistically independent. It is shown that this approximation breaks down in the extreme near-field regime, where hybridization of surface phonon-polaritons across nanometric vacuum gaps generates finite fluctuating-current cross correlations between opposite interfaces. Using a microscopic coupled-oscillator model combined with a Green-tensor formulation of the Poynting vector, the resulting correlation-induced correction to radiative heat transfer is derived. For polar materials, these correlations become significant when the hybridization energy approaches the intrinsic damping rate and can substantially modify conventional fluctuational-electrodynamics predictions at subnanometric separations.
item.dc:creator: Philippe Ben-Abdallah

item.title: Emergence of Gaussian entanglement and non-Gaussianity in high-harmonic generation driven by bright squeezed light
item.description: arXiv:2606.22714v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: High harmonic generation (HHG) is a highly nonlinear optical process in which radiation from a strong driving field is up-converted into its high-order harmonics. In atomic systems, this nonlinearity manifests itself through the intensity scaling of the emitted harmonics with the driving field strength. Despite the highly nonlinear nature of HHG, when the driving field is prepared in a classical Gaussian state and atomic depletion remains negligible, the quantum statistical properties of the generated harmonics retains classical Gaussian quantum statistics. Driving HHG with bright squeezed vacuum (BSV) light challenges this paradigm, as its enhanced field fluctuations can modify the statistical properties of the generated harmonics. In this work, we investigate the conditions under which BSV-driven HHG gives rise to non-classical Gaussian states, and identify the regimes where this Gaussian description breaks down. For bichromatic driving by a strong coherent field at frequency $\omega$ and a perturbative BSV field at $2\omega$, the even-harmonic response is approximately linear in the BSV quadrature, leading to non-classical multimode Gaussian entanglement in the harmonic field. We show that this state can be described as a distributed collective squeezed mode over the even-harmonic manifold, and characterize its covariance matrix, entanglement structure, and quantum teleportation fidelity as an operational benchmark. Our results highlight the potential of non-classically driven HHG as a platform for engineering Gaussian and non-Gaussian states of light in the extreme ultraviolet regime.

item.title: Nonlinear Tellegen limit
item.description: arXiv:2607.10584v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The Tellegen limit is the fundamental electromagnetic stability bound on magnetoelectric media. We show that nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling gives rise to a new Tellegen limit, which we term the \textit{nonlinear Tellegen limit}. Unlike the linear Tellegen limit, which is fixed by material parameters, the nonlinear Tellegen limit is field-tunable -- a static electric or magnetic field drives the system toward electromagnetic instability at a material-specific critical field determined by the symmetry-allowed nonlinear magnetoelectric couplings and electromagnetic response. The approach to this limit is accompanied by a field-tunable linear birefringence, whose maximum is bounded by the nonlinear Tellegen limit -- beyond which the medium becomes electromagnetically unstable. We demonstrate the nonlinear Tellegen limit and the field-space stability phase diagram in two magnetically ordered material systems -- a $d$-wave altermagnet and an M-type hexagonal ferrite -- showing that the symmetry of the magnetic point group governs both the structure of the nonlinear magnetoelectric tensor and the resulting electromagnetic instability.
